regras.titulo: has an .editorconfig

porque.texto: Portuguese on purpose: tooling/verify/prove-steps.mjs matches the line below byte for byte — the `titulo` key plus this exact title — to plant its sentinel and prove the MCP freshness gate. Translating it drops that proof in silence, and repeating the literal up here would make the proof's `replace` hit this comment instead of the title.

provas.porque: Without .editorconfig each editor rewrites indentation and line endings on its own, and in a Windows repository that becomes a CRLF diff in a file nobody touched. The two trees are identical except for that file: if the rule stops looking at it, the fail side exits 0 and the proof accuses.

regras.titulo: automated dependency updates

porque.texto: A read guard only: applicability is still the ROOT package.json, because dependabot and renovate are repository configuration and not package configuration. Without the guard, breaking the package.json took this rule out of the denominator along with the other three.

provas.porque: An npm project with neither dependabot nor renovate piles up CVEs in a transitive dependency with nobody opening a PR. Both trees have package.json — without it the rule falls into not-applicable and the proof would prove nothing — and they differ only by .github/dependabot.yml.

The N/A branch `not an npm project` leaves the DENOMINATOR, and a branch that leaves the denominator is the place where the score climbs with nobody fixing anything — that is how the broken package.json turned 9 of 10 into 6 of 6. While the runner read the exit code, this branch could not be locked: `na` and `passou` both exit 0. The `pass` side is a tree with no package.json at all and has to come out N/A, not `passou`: dependabot and renovate are npm-project configuration, and charging that to a repository that is not npm would be inventing debt. With the mutation `na(...)` → `null`, this side becomes `passou` and the case accuses.

regras.titulo: has CI

provas.porque: A repository with no workflow at all has no gate: what gets through is whatever the author remembered to run on his own machine. The rule reads the list tracked by git, so the pass side also proves that a workflow only counts once committed — an untracked file does not count.

regras.titulo: the CI reaches the verification the repository has

porque.texto: Same read guard as the others: with a broken package.json, `r.pkg?.scripts` became `{}`, `alvos` came out empty and the rule left the denominator. Four rules vanishing is what turned 9 of 10 into 6 of 6. Charges only what the repository HAS. Demanding `lint` of a repo with no lint is demanding it adopt a tool — a decision of another level.

THE GATE SCRIPTS ARE IN THE LIST, and leaving them out cost the rule its own author: the rebar declares `verify` and not `lint`/`typecheck`/`test`, so this rule — the one that is the whole point of the project — came out NOT APPLICABLE on the rebar itself. It was exercised in the proofs and in the generated project, never on the owner.

`check` AND `validate` ARE DELIBERATELY OUT, and the measurement is why. The first draft had them, and it failed on the first repository it was tried against — this one: the rebar declares `check` as `node tooling/rebar-check/index.mjs .`, and the CI runs that exact command through the `self` step of the gate. The rule sees the NAME and cannot read through `verify.config.mjs`, so it accused a repository that does run the thing. False positive, on the author, on the first try.

And the case that seemed to justify them does not need them: in the forensics the `openparts` had a `check` chaining everything and nothing ran it — but it had NO CI at all, so the `ci` rule already fails it and this one correctly returns N/A pointing there. Widening recovered no lost case; it only added false-positive surface. Automatic rule that is wrong costs more than a missing rule.
`verify`/`verificar` stay because they name THE GATE, unambiguously, and bilingual for the same reason as `PASTA_TESTE`: the audited repositories are Brazilian.

provas.porque: This proof locks the false positive already measured in prior-standard: the previous version looked for the literal words lint/typecheck/test in the YAML and failed every repository that aggregates verification into a single command. The pass side has a workflow that contains NONE of the three words — it calls only `npm run verificar`, which chains `estatica` (lint + typecheck) and `test`, exercising two levels of the expansion — and it has to PASS. The two package.json are byte for byte identical: the only variable is the workflow's `run:` line, so the fail side can only fail because the CI really does not reach the verification the repository has.

P1 from an external audit, reproduced before fixing: with `scripts.test` defined and a workflow that only does `echo ok`, the rule failed -- and adding the line `# TODO: run test later` flipped the verdict to PASSED, exit 0. The base text was the raw YAML, so the word anywhere in the file satisfied the rule. The fail side has exactly that tree: a comment citing test, a job named test, and an `echo "running tests"` -- the three neighbors the report names together, and none of them executes anything. The pass side has all THREE too, plus a real `run: npm test`: it is the proof that the fix was not taking the word out of the text, but looking only where the workflow executes. Whoever swaps `comandosDoCi` for a subtraction of comments turns the fail side green again by the job name.

A Windows checkout writes CRLF (`core.autocrlf=true` is the Git for Windows default), and the extractor matched each line with `(.*)$`, where `.` does not match ``: not one `run:` line matched, the extracted text was EMPTY, and a CI that runs the lint was accused of not reaching it. Measured on `expressjs/cors`, whose only changed verdict between a CRLF and an LF clone was this one. Both workflows here are CRLF on purpose, and `.gitattributes` marks them `-text` so the repository's own `eol=lf` cannot turn them back into LF — without that the case would pass on a tree that no longer reproduces the defect. The `pass` side runs `npm run lint`; the `fail` side runs `npm run build` under a step NAMED `lint`. Whoever removes the normalization turns `pass` red; whoever answers an empty extraction by falling back to the raw YAML turns `fail` green, because the word is still there in `name:`.

O vocabulario da regra era `lint`, `typecheck` e `test`, e com isso ela saia NAO-APLICAVEL no proprio rebar -- que declara `verify`. A regra que e o diferencial do projeto nao se aplicava ao projeto: era exercitada nas provas e no projeto gerado, nunca no dono. `verify` e `verificar` entram porque nomeiam O PORTAO, sem ambiguidade, e bilingue pelo mesmo motivo do PASTA_TESTE: os repositorios auditados sao brasileiros. `check` e `validate` ficaram DE FORA, e a medicao e o motivo: o primeiro rascunho os tinha e reprovou no primeiro repositorio em que foi testado, este -- o rebar declara `check` como `node tooling/rebar-check/index.mjs .` e o CI roda esse comando exato pelo passo `self` do portao. A regra ve o NOME e nao le atraves do verify.config.mjs, entao acusou quem de fato roda a coisa. E o caso que parecia justifica-los nao precisa deles: o openparts tinha `check` que ninguem rodava, mas nao tinha CI nenhum, entao a regra `ci` ja o reprova e esta aqui devolve N/A apontando para la. Ampliar nao recuperou caso perdido, so acrescentou superficie de falso positivo. O lado aprovar tem `check` E `verify`, com o CI alcancando so o `verify`: quem reintroduzir `check` na lista faz ele ficar vermelho.

BOTH N/A branches of this rule in a single case, one per folder — the folders are called `pass` and `fail` by inheritance from the format, and here each isolates a different branch. `pass/` has the lint and test scripts and no workflow: the one that charges for the existence of CI is the `ci` rule, and charging twice for the same absence measures the same thing twice and fails the repository double. `fail/` has a workflow and a package.json whose only script is `empacotar`: the rule only charges for what the repository HAS, because demanding `lint` from someone who has no lint is demanding the adoption of a tool, a decision of another level. Either of the two turning into `passou` makes the case accuse.

Measured on 2026-09-17 on `motdotla/dotenv`: `the CI does not reach: lint`, with `.github/workflows/ci.yml` running `npm test` and the `test` script being `npm run build && npm run lint && npm run dts-check && tap run …`. The lint runs on every push. The expansion did not follow it because `npm test` is npm's LIFECYCLE SHORTHAND — there is no `run` in it — and the invocation expression demanded the literal word. The two trees here run the same `npm ci` and the same `npm test`; only the body of `test` changes, and with it whether the chain reaches the lint. TWO LOCKS IN ONE CASE, because `npm ci` is on both sides and there is a script CALLED `ci` on both sides, chaining the lint: whoever reads any bare token after a package manager as a script name makes the fail side green, and buys `npm ci` — the most common line there is in a CI — as proof that a repository runs whatever a script of that name chains. `npm ci` is the clean install, not that script.

The expansion followed `npm run x` into the BODY of the script and stopped at `node <file>`. Measured on 2026-08-30: `repo-d` was accused of "the CI does not reach: lint" with `.github/workflows/verificar.yml` running `npm run verificar`, the `verificar` script being `node ci/verificar.mjs`, and that file running `npm run --silent lint` on line 21. The real chain has three links and the expansion walked two — stopping at the `node` was declaring that the CI does not reach the lint it reaches on every run. Both sides have the SAME workflow, the SAME package.json and the SAME runner: only the list of steps INSIDE the runner changes.

Measured on 2026-09-17 on `browserbase/stagehand`: `the CI does not reach: lint, typecheck`, with `.github/workflows/ci.yml` running `pnpm check` and `check` being `turbo run fmt:check lint typecheck`. TWO LINKS WERE MISSING, and the deliberate exclusion of the names `check` and `validate` is NOT one of them: that exclusion governs what the rule DEMANDS (`alvos`), never what it expands, and the expansion resolves any declared script by name. What was missing was (1) `pnpm <name>`, which the invocation expression never matched — its alternatives already ate the space after the manager and the `\s+` outside the group demanded another one, so of the four spellings it named only the npm ones ever worked — and (2) a task runner's `run`, which hands a LIST of names to the tasks of the same manifest. The two trees run the same `pnpm install` and the same `pnpm check`; only the task `check` names changes, from the one that chains lint and typecheck to the one that builds. Whoever restores the old expression, or drops the `turbo run`/`nx run-many` branch, turns the pass side red.

regras.titulo: has tests

provas.porque: Locks one of the two deterministic false positives already measured: the rule was blind to a test named in Portuguese — 43 tracked files with `prova` in the name in the prior-standard and the rule saw ZERO, in a checker written in Portuguese. This variant isolates the PATH SEGMENT branch: the only test file on the pass side is `provas/soma.mjs`, and no file name would match on its own. If the `provas` segment leaves the recognizer, the pass side exits 1. The Portuguese folder name stays: it is PASTA_TESTE vocabulary, what the recognizer searches for inside third-party repositories.

P2 #6 of the external audit. `ehTeste` looked at the name only, and a document name falls into BOTH recognizers: `provas/PLANO.md` gets in through the folder, which is in PASTA_TESTE, and `PLANO.teste.md` gets in through NOME_TESTE. The result is a false PASS -- a repository with zero tests and one planning document passed the rule. The `tests__python-name` case had already recorded that `TESTE-1-cabo-KKL.md` does not count, but attributed that to the `-` separator instead of the extension; renaming it to `TESTE.1.cabo.md` was enough to bring the hole back. The fix is a DENIAL of document extensions, and not a list of extensions that count: an allowlist would fail `.dart`, `.R`, `.jl`, `.hs` and `.bats`, and saying "zero test files" to someone who wrote tests costs more than the missing rule. That is why the pass side has a `.bats` -- it goes red if someone swaps the denial for an allowlist. `provas`, `teste` and `TESTE` stay Portuguese: they are the PASTA_TESTE and NOME_TESTE vocabulary.

The other half of the same false positive. This variant isolates the FILE NAME branch: the only test on the pass side is `provar-soma.mjs`, at the root, with no test folder in the path. It exists separately because the previous version of this proof had both branches in the same tree — and, restoring the Portuguese-blindness by hand, it stayed GREEN, because the other branch still matched. A proof that survives the return of the defect it locks is not a proof. `provar-` stays Portuguese: it is a NOME_TESTE alternative.

The name pattern knew only the dot (`.test.`), and the Python and Go convention writes the separator with an underscore. Measured on 2026-08-30: `repo-v` was accused of "zero test files" while having three tracked `*_test.py` scripts, among them `02-obd-kline/vectra_kw82_test.py`. It is the same vocabulary blindness that already cost this rule a false positive in Portuguese — 43 files with "prova" in the name and zero seen. Both sides have the SAME module; only the test file beside it changes. `TESTE-1-cabo-KKL.md` from the same repository still does NOT count, and that is why the accepted separator is `_` and not `-`.

regras.titulo: has a typecheck script

porque.texto: A DECLARATION IS NOT SOURCE. Measured on 2026-09-16: `sindresorhus/slugify`

3.0.2 ships `index.js` with a hand-written `index.d.ts`, runs `xo && ava`, and was accused of "no tracked package.json has script typecheck". There is no TypeScript there to compile — the only `.ts` file is the contract a JavaScript package publishes for its consumers. What can go wrong with it, the declaration drifting from `index.js`, is caught by a type TEST (`tsd`, `expect-type`), which is a decision of another level; demanding a `typecheck` script charges the repository for a practice it has no code for. One `.ts` or `.tsx` that is not a declaration and the rule applies again.

provas.porque: A TypeScript project whose only contact with the compiler is the build: the type error only shows up when someone tries to package, or in production, never in a check CI can call on its own.

A JavaScript package that publishes a hand-written declaration has no TypeScript to compile. Measured on `sindresorhus/slugify` 3.0.2: `index.js` plus `index.d.ts`, `xo && ava`, and the rule accused it of having no typecheck script. Both sides have the SAME package.json with no typecheck script, the SAME `index.js` and the SAME `index.d.ts`; the `fail` side adds ONE real TypeScript source file, `src/normalizar.ts`. The `pass` side has to come out N/A and the `fail` side keeps failing: whoever removes the declaration branch turns `pass` into a failure, and whoever widens it to any repository that HAS a `.d.ts` turns `fail` into N/A, which would hide every TypeScript project that also ships declarations.

A TEMPLATE IS NOT A PRODUCT, the same lesson as the caso.json one floor above. A repository that carries the generator also carries the .tsx files the generator COPIES into the created project — files that are not compiled here, that have no tsconfig here, and that made rebar itself drop from 11 of 11 to 11 of 13 the moment new/ was tracked (measured on 2026-08-31 on a mirror of the repository in os.tmpdir()). The pass side has the modelo.json marker at the template root and the rule leaves the denominator; the fail side is the SAME tree without the marker, and the rule accuses. Whoever deletes the exclusion makes the pass side go red; whoever turns the exclusion into an unconditional bypass makes the fail side go green. `modelo.json` stays Portuguese: it is the literal marker file name the generator writes.

The two N/A branches of the rule, one per folder. `pass/` has `src/app.ts` — real TypeScript — and NO package.json: with no manifest there is no script to invoke, and the rule asks for a target CI can call. `fail/` has the package.json and no .ts or .tsx file at all: charging a project that has no types for a type check is accusing by vocabulary. The presence of TypeScript on the side with no manifest is deliberate, and it is what makes each folder isolate ONE branch: without it the `pass` side would be N/A for two reasons at once, and the mutation of either one would still find the other in front of it. Each branch has to be the only path on its side, or the proof does not say which of them locked.

Demanding a script named exactly `typecheck` charged the repository for the VOCABULARY and not for the practice — the same mistake the `tests` rule made with Portuguese file names, in a checker written in Portuguese. Measured: prumo (`"tipos": "tsc -b"`) and repo-d (`"tipos"` at the root and `"typecheck"` in three packages) were accused of having no typecheck while both had the script. This variant isolates the NAME branch: the `pass` side has `tipos` and nothing else. The accepted list is still a list of script NAMES, and the `fail` side shows why — it runs `tsc -b` INSIDE `empacotar`, which is exactly the failure the base case describes (the only contact with the compiler is the build) and it keeps failing. That is what preserved the true accusation against navesz.github.io, whose `build` is `npm run data && tsc --noEmit && vite build`. `tipos` and `empacotar` stay Portuguese: they are the script names the rule has to accept in a Brazilian repository, and the whole point of this case.

The LOCK on the template exclusion, which is what separates an escape hatch from a bypass. The marker only holds when its prefix is EXACTLY a known template root. On the pass side it is at new/site/blocks/ and the tree leaves the evaluation; on the fail side the same file is one level below, at new/site/blocks/app/, and it has to be REFUSED — the tree stays evaluated and the rule accuses. Without that lock, a modelo.json in any folder would hide any tree, which was exactly the three-byte attack the caso.json accepted once already.

regras.titulo: the formatting is checked, not only rewritten

porque.texto: The title says CHECKED and not "has", because "has" was the defect. See the section next to `NOMES_TYPECHECK` for the measurement that moved it.

The CI enters as a source alongside the scripts, and not instead of them: a repository may gate the formatting with a bare `- run: npx prettier --check .` and declare no script at all. Reading only package.json would accuse that repository of what it is doing right — the "defense looked for where the defect was found" family. WRITE, THEN VERIFY: the formatter ran and, after it and in the same job, a step fails on the dirty tree. It is the third shape of enforcing the formatting, and reading only the command was calling it a writer. See `escreveEConfere` for the measurement and for the three locks. The dependency is checked ONLY on the failing path, and this order is the point: the check is what the rule wants, the declaration is only how it tells the two accusations apart. A repository that checks through `npx` without declaring the package is already past, above.

provas.porque: An npm project that has a linter and no formatter at all: each machine reindents the file its own way and the review diff becomes whitespace noise instead of a change of behavior. The `pass` side declares prettier AND a script that checks with it — since 2026-09-07 the rule wants an invocation that can fail, and a side that only rewrote would certify the very hole `formatter__write-is-not-check` names. The write script stays next to the check on purpose: having both is the normal shape and the rule must not punish it.

NO TOOL IS HARDCODED, and this repository has no prettier at all. `biome ci` is read-only by contract — the mode biome documents for the gate — and a repository that adopted biome instead of prettier is not less formatted for it. The `fail` side is the same repository with `biome check --write .` alone, and the flag is the whole point: `biome check` on its own DOES gate, and `--write` is what turns the very same subcommand into a writer that comes back green. Reading the subcommand and ignoring the flag would certify it. It is the biome spelling of the `assay` defect, and it locks the second half of the rule — each family is judged by ITS OWN writing mode, not by a list of flags borrowed from prettier. Both sides keep the write script for the same reason as `formatter__write-is-not-check`: having a way to reformat is normal.

THE FALSE POSITIVE ON THE AUTHOR, and it is not hypothetical: rebar's own script is `node node_modules/prettier/bin/prettier.cjs --check .`, written that way because `npx prettier` is not the same command on both systems of the CI matrix. A rule that matched a command STARTING with `prettier`, or that split on whitespace and read the first token, would have failed the repository that ships the rule — the third time this project would have been caught demanding a spelling instead of a practice, after `NOMES_TYPECHECK` and the shadcn `tailwind-merge`. The `pass` side is that script; the `fail` side is the same invocation through the same path with `--write`, so the two trees differ in one flag and the case can only go green if what is being read is the MODE and not the shape of the call.

THE CHECK DOES NOT HAVE TO BE A SCRIPT. A repository may gate the formatting with a bare `- run: npx prettier --check .` in the workflow and declare in package.json only the `format` that rewrites — and it IS gating: the pull request goes red. Reading package.json alone would accuse it, which is the "defense looked for where the defect was found" family that already produced five false findings in this ruler. The `fail` side is the same repository with the same line COMMENTED OUT inside the block scalar, and it is there because of `ci-gates__comment-is-not-execution`: a comment mentions a command and runs nothing, and a rule that grep'd the raw YAML would take the mention for the practice. The two workflows differ in one `#`.

THE THIRD FAMILY, and it is here because a mutation caught its absence: with the dprint branch deleted from the rule, the suite stayed 65 of 65 green — a branch nobody proved is a branch nobody can be sure of. dprint spells the two modes as SUBCOMMANDS and not as flags: `dprint check` reports and comes back non-zero, `dprint fmt` rewrites and comes back zero. So the `fail` side owns the formatter, runs it, and gates on nothing — the dprint spelling of `prettier --write`; the `pass` side adds `dprint check` next to it. It is the same pair as `formatter__biome`, on a tool whose vocabulary shares no word with prettier’s, which is the point of having three.

FORMATTING CHECKED BY THE LINTER, with no dedicated formatter in the repository. `@stylistic/eslint-plugin` is where eslint's layout rules went when core dropped them, so `eslint .` here comes back non-zero on a badly formatted file — the practice the rule wants, by a fourth road. A rule that demanded prettier, biome or dprint by name would accuse this repository of having no formatter while it fails the build on formatting, which is the exact error the `@radix-ui` rule made against the only one of six repositories that had got it right. The `fail` side is the same repository with `eslint . --fix`: the plugin is still declared, but `--fix` rewrites the layout and comes back green, so nothing gates — the eslint spelling of `prettier --write`. It also locks the guard against the cheap version of this branch: accepting any `eslint` invocation would pass `assay`, which has eslint and eslint-config-next and no formatting rule turned on at all.

The same class as `ui-falso__monorepo`, on the dependency axis: the rule read only `dependencies`/`devDependencies` from the ROOT. Measured, openkartline was accused of "no prettier, biome or dprint" while being a pnpm workspace with `"prettier": "^3.4.2"` in apps/web/package.json and two scripts (`format`, `format:check`) that call it. The root of a monorepo usually declares no dependency at all — it is just the map of the workspaces. Here the raw union of all manifests is the right match, and in `ui-falso` it is not: the package manager hoists the formatter to the whole workspace, so declaring prettier in one package formats the entire repository, while a `components.json` configures the aliases of one project only. The two roots are identical; only the package's manifest changes. The check script lives in the package too, and that is the second thing this case locks: the rule now judges the BODY of the scripts, and a version that read the scripts of the root manifest alone would accuse openkartline all over again, one layer down.

Prettier, biome and dprint are npm dependencies: with no manifest there is nowhere to declare them, and the rule has no object to check. The `pass` side is a tree with JavaScript code and no package.json, and has to come out N/A and not `passou` — passing would be certifying as formatted a repository nobody looked into at all. The `fail` side proves the guard did not swallow the rule: with the manifest present and only eslint declared, the accusation still comes out.

The vocabulary was four families — prettier, biome, dprint and eslint with a layout plugin — and a repository whose formatter belongs to another language was told it has none. Measured on 2026-09-17 on `biomejs/biome`, which is an npm project and therefore inside this rule: `.github/workflows/main.yml` runs `cargo fmt --all --verbose -- --check`, which is a check outright, and `autofix.yml` runs `cargo fmt --all` followed by `autofix-ci/action`, which is the write-then-verify shape. It gates its formatting TWICE and the accusation was `script lint, lint only rewrites`. Rejecting a repository for enforcing formatting, because the enforcement is written in another language's tool, is the same mistake this rule already paid for with `tailwind-merge` and with `@radix-ui`. The two sides here differ in the flag rustfmt reads: `-- --check` fails on a badly formatted file, and the bare form REWRITES it in silence — the same writer-is-not-a-checker line that opened this rule. Both sides declare prettier and a `format` that only rewrites, so what decides the verdict is the cargo line and nothing else.

TWO PACKAGES, ONE SCRIPT NAME, DIFFERENT BODIES — the shape that decides how `scriptsDeTodos` may return its answer. The root of the workspace declares `format` rewriting everything; `apps/web` declares `format` checking. Collecting the scripts into a map keyed by NAME loses one of the two bodies, and it loses the one read first: git lists `apps/web/package.json` before `package.json`, so the root’s writer overwrites the package’s checker and the rule accuses a repository that gates. That is why the helper returns PAIRS. The `fail` side is the same two packages with both `format` scripts rewriting — the collision is still there, and now nothing checks, so it must fail. Between them, the pair pins that the rule reads EVERY body and not one per name.

A file that EXISTS and cannot be read can never become N/A, because N/A leaves the denominator and the score GOES UP. The old `lerJson` merged "does not exist" with "exists and is broken" into a `catch { return null }`, and `pkg === null` became `na('not an npm project')`. Measured in the attack: a repository at 9 of 10 (90%) with a syntactically broken package.json became 6 of 6 (100%) — dependabot, ci-gateia, typecheck and formatter vanished from the score and it started taking maximum marks. Breaking the file improved the score. The `fail` side HAS prettier AND a script that checks with it, declared in apps/web/package.json, and even so it has to fail: what could not be read is not certified. It is that presence that makes the proof bite, and it is why the check script was added to the fail side when the rule was tightened on 2026-09-07 — without it that side would start failing for want of a checker, the unreadable-manifest guard could be deleted whole and this case would stay green, proving nothing. The two trees are identical except for the trailing comma and the brace that does not close at the root.

THE DEFECT THIS RULE WAS TIGHTENED FOR, copied from what was measured on 2026-09-07. The `fail` side carries the manifest of `assay`: prettier declared, one formatting script, and the script is `prettier --write "**/*.{ts,tsx}"`. The old rule read dependencies only and printed `formatter · has a formatter` on a repository where `prettier --check .` accused 32 files — `navesz-portfolio` 10, `rebar-site` 12. `--write` cannot fail: it rewrites the file and comes back zero, so nothing gates on it, and the glob does not even reach the `.mjs` and `.json` where most of those files were. It is the same shape the project already wrote down about openparts: a script that chained everything and that nothing ever ran. The second script of the `fail` side, `prettier --write --list-different .`, is not decoration: with `--write` on, `--list-different` prints the files prettier REWROTE and still exits zero, so a rule that hunted for the checking flag anywhere in the line would take a writer for a gate. It is what makes the writing modes load-bearing and not a comment. The `pass` side carries the NAMED FALSE POSITIVE: the same repository plus `prettier --list-different .` on its own, prettier's other checking flag — it prints the paths and comes back non-zero, exactly like `--check`. A rule that hardcoded the string `--check` would fail a repository that is doing the right thing by another spelling, and the `prettier-plugin-tailwindcss` sitting in both sides is the smaller trap: it carries the word `prettier` and is not the CLI. Both sides keep the write script, because owning one is normal and must never be what accuses you.

WRITE, THEN VERIFY is a third shape of enforcing the formatting, and reading only the command called it a writer. Measured on 2026-09-17 on `e2b-dev/e2b`: `script format, format, format only rewrites — nothing fails when a file is out of format`, with `.github/workflows/lint.yml` running `pnpm run format` and then, in the same job, `if [[ -n $(git status --porcelain) ]]; then … exit 1`. A badly formatted file turns the run red there; the enforcement is not in the script, it is in the PAIR. The formatter is resolved THROUGH the script, because `pnpm run format` is not a literal CLI invocation and demanding the literal one would miss every monorepo that aggregates it — e2b's case, where the four `format` scripts calling `prettier --write` live in the packages and the workflow calls only the root one. The two sides here differ in one step, the last one. The `git diff --exit-code -- esquema.json` over generated code is on BOTH sides and is the ORDER lock: a gate BEFORE the formatter proves nothing about formatting, and whoever asks only "is there a formatter and is there a tree gate in this job" makes the fail side green with a step that has nothing to do with format.

The claim write-then-verify makes is about ONE RUN, so the pair has to meet inside the same job. Both sides here have the same two jobs, the same `npm run format` and the same `git diff --exit-code`; what changes is which job the gate lives in. On the fail side the formatter runs in `formato` and dies with the runner, and the `git diff --exit-code` of `testar` runs on a clean checkout that no formatter ever touched — it can never come out dirty, and it enforces nothing about formatting. Whoever reads the workflow, or the repository, as one text lets two strangers vouch for each other and turns the whole mechanism into a bypass: any repository with a formatter somewhere and a `git diff --exit-code` over generated code anywhere would pass.

regras.titulo: reads env and documents it in .env.example

porque.texto: Asked LAST, and only about what is about to be accused: the write scan costs a read of the tracked Python, Ruby and shell, and nobody pays for it on the green path. A variable the repository writes into an environment itself is not documentation anyone owes — see `escritasDeEnv` for the measurement on `oraios/serena`.

provas.porque: An environment variable that the code reads and the .env.example does not list: whoever clones the repository only finds out it exists when the application breaks at runtime, and a half-done .env.example is worse than its absence because it looks complete.

Reported in issue #28: a Vite repository reading `import.meta.env.DEV`, `MODE` and `BASE_URL` was told they were not documented, and they cannot be — the bundler replaces them with literals at build time, and writing `DEV=` into `.env.example` would put something false into the document. Both sides have the SAME `.env.example` documenting `VITE_API_URL`, and the SAME file reading all five built-ins plus that variable. The ONLY difference is one read: `pass` takes `MODE` from `import.meta.env`, `fail` takes it from `process.env`, where it is an ordinary environment variable in a Node program and has to be documented. Whoever drops the exclusion turns `pass` red; whoever excludes the names regardless of namespace turns `fail` green.

The rule exists for the half-done .env.example, which is worse than its absence because it looks complete. But a repository that reads no variable at all owes nobody a .env.example: demanding it would create an empty ceremonial file in every project. The `pass` side has real code and zero `process.env`, and has to come out N/A. The `fail` side reads `API_TOKEN` and does not have the file, so the guard cannot have become an escape hatch for the whole rule.

`.env.example` documents what a person has to FILL IN, and nobody fills in `NO_COLOR` in an example file: what defines it is the terminal, and what defines `CI` is the runner. Measured on 2026-08-30, two of the six accused were only this — `prior-standard` became "reads 1 environment variable(s) and has no .env.example" with `NO_COLOR` as the repository's only variable, and `prumo` was charged for `NO_COLOR` while having a `.env.example` with `PRUMO_KEK` and `DATABASE_URL` documented. The `pass` side reads ONLY environment variables and has to come out N/A; the `fail` side reads the same ones PLUS a project variable and keeps failing, so that the sieve does not become an escape hatch for the whole rule.

Measured on 2026-09-17 on `Skyvern-AI/skyvern`: `not documented: VITE_API_BASE_URL, VITE_WSS_BASE_URL, VITE_ENABLE_LOG_ARTIFACTS` — all three are in `skyvern-frontend/.env.example`, which is WHERE THEY BELONG, because Vite reads the env from the package directory and a `VITE_` written into a root file would not reach the build. The rule read `<root>/.env.example` and nothing else, so the monorepo that documented it in the right place was accused of not documenting it: 12 variables accused, of which 7 were documented. It is the "defect looked for recursively, defense looked for only at the root" family, for the fourth time in this ruler. The climb is the same one `ui-falso` makes, and this case is what keeps it from becoming "anywhere": the two trees hold the same `web/src/configuracao.ts`, the same root `.env.example` and the same file documenting the two variables — only the FOLDER it sits in changes, from `web/`, which is above the reader, to `outro/`, which is a sibling and reaches nothing. Whoever accepts any `.env.example` in the repository turns the fail side green and buys an unrelated package's file as documentation.

`.env.example` documents what the program READS AT RUN TIME, and a variable cited in a comment is read by nobody. This is not hypothetical: while writing the note for the `url-producao` fix in this repository, the example sentence with `process` `.env` made rebar itself fail on `env-example`, charging for two variables that exist nowhere. It is the same trap that already cost the ruler a rule — of the seven occurrences the literal-color rule turned up in prior-app, five were comments documenting the rule itself. Both sides have the SAME comment citing the SAME variable: on the `fail` side it is also genuinely read.

A WRITE IN A TEST IS A STUB, NOT A SUPPLY, and this cost a measurement to learn. The first version of the write exemption read the test files too, and on `browserbase/stagehand` it silently dropped `HERMES_SESSION_PLATFORM` and `OPENCLAW_SHELL` from the accusation, because `packages/cli/tests/agent.test.ts` does `process.env.HERMES_SESSION_PLATFORM = "telegram"` to stage the case. In production those two come from OUTSIDE — from the agent whose presence they detect — and they are exactly what a `.env.example` exists to announce. A test stating what it wants the environment to look like is the opposite of the repository supplying the value. The two trees here have the same source, the same test and the same stub of both variables; only one line of the `.env.example` changes. Whoever lets the scan read the tests makes the fail side green, and buys the exemption with a line in a test — the same hole the secret scanner refuses under the name "any line in a test file".

Measured on 2026-09-17 on `oraios/serena`: `not documented: SERENA_SOLIDITY_STATE_DIR`, and the accusation is INVERTED. That variable is not read from the user's environment — serena WRITES it, in `src/solidlsp/language_servers/solidity_language_server.py` (`launch_env["SERENA_SOLIDITY_STATE_DIR"] = state_dir`), into the environment of a child process it launches itself, and the only thing that reads it is `solidity_homedir_preload.cjs`, the preload of that child. It is an internal channel between two processes of the same repository, and telling the person who clones it to fill that in in a `.env.example` is worse than a missing rule: it is a wrong instruction. THE WRITE IS IN ANOTHER LANGUAGE, which is the whole difficulty — the rule discovers variables in JavaScript, because `process.env.X` is a JavaScript shape, and the write can be anywhere. The two trees here are identical down to the `.env.example`, the `.cjs` that reads and the Python file's name; what changes is the DIRECTION of one line, from `launch_env["APP_STATE_DIR"] = …` to `… = launch_env["APP_STATE_DIR"]`. Whoever exempts on the mere MENTION of the name, instead of on the assignment, makes the fail side green — and there the value does have to come from outside.

regras.titulo: has a LICENSE

provas.porque: package.json declaring "license" without the LICENSE file in the repository: the metadata promises a grant of use the repository does not deliver, and whoever clones it receives no right in writing.

regras.titulo: has a README

porque.texto: THIS RULE CATCHES ZERO TODAY, and that is written here on purpose.

Measured on 31/08/2026 across the 12 repositories on this machine: ALL have a README, from 25 to 282 useful lines, and NONE is framework boilerplate (I searched for "bootstrapped with create-next-app", "npm create vite", "Getting Started with Create React App" and the like — zero occurrences).

So why it exists. First: two hours before this line was written, rebar itself was the only repository with no README, and it went public that way — while docs/PLANO.md listed "README como entregável" [README as a deliverable] TWICE as a hole this project exists to fill. The ruler could not see the hole its own plan named. Second: the generator is going to produce a new repository, and a new repository is born without a README by default.

PRESENCE only, with no size floor. A line limit would fail `navesz.github.io` (25 lines) and `repo-v` (31), which are small projects with a proportional README — and a wrong automatic rule costs more than a missing rule.

provas.porque: rebar itself went public without a README, while docs/PLANO.md listed "README as a deliverable" twice as a hole it exists to close. The ruler could not see the hole its own plan named. This proof locks that from coming back — and locks the generator too, which will produce new repositories, and a new repository is born without a README.

regras.titulo: Apache-2.0 accompanied by a NOTICE

provas.porque: Distribution under Apache-2.0 without the NOTICE file: section 4(d) of the license itself requires passing the NOTICE along, so the repository is at odds with the license it declares.

The two N/A branches of the rule, one per folder. `pass/` has no LICENSE: a missing license is the failure of the `license` rule, and accusing here again would count the same debt twice in the denominator. `fail/` has an MIT LICENSE: the obligation to pass the NOTICE along comes from section 4(d) of Apache-2.0 and from no other license, so demanding it of an MIT project would be inventing a clause it never signed. The two sides come out N/A for different reasons, and swapping either one for `passou` makes the case accuse. `passou` stays Portuguese: it is the state value prove.mjs matches on (prove.mjs:198-200), not prose.

regras.titulo: git hook committed with the execute bit

porque.texto: AUDIT FINDING, 31/08: mode 100755 was guaranteed ONCE, at creation, and nothing kept it. A `git update-index --chmod=-x` — or a file created on Windows, where the bit does not exist — returns the hook to 100644, and on Linux git starts IGNORING IT in silence. The gate declares itself on and does nothing, which is the worst possible state.
The mode read is the INDEX's, not the disk's: a local `chmod` does not travel in the clone, and it is the clone that lands on the user's machine.

WHAT THE RULE ASKS IS NOT "be executable", IT IS "git can run you". The two were the same thing until husky 9, and taking them for the same thing accused `mastra-ai/mastra` — measured on 2026-09-17 — of a hook that runs on every commit there. See `huskyV9` for the mechanism and for the version, which is the whole of the difference.

provas.porque: Audit finding on 31/08: the 100755 mode of the hooks was guaranteed once, at creation, and nothing kept it there. A `git update-index --chmod=-x` — or a file created on Windows, where the bit does not exist — puts the hook back to 100644, and on Linux git starts IGNORING IT in silence: the installer prints "hooks installed" and nothing runs. The gate declares itself on and does nothing, which is the worst possible state. The mode checked is the INDEX one, because a local `chmod` does not travel in the clone.

The exemption SUBTRACTS the husky-managed hooks, it does not turn the rule off. Both sides declare husky 9 and both carry a `.husky/pre-commit` at 100644, which is right there and is not accused; what changes is `tooling/hooks/pre-push`, a hook with a shebang, in a committed directory, of the kind `core.hooksPath` points at and git runs DIRECTLY — 100755 on the pass side, 100644 on the fail side. It is rebar's own layout, and rebar is the true positive this rule must keep catching. Whoever reads `.husky/` plus husky in the manifest as `na` FOR THE WHOLE REPOSITORY makes the fail side green and buys silence about a real mute gate with the presence of an unrelated dependency.

Measured on 2026-09-17 on `mastra-ai/mastra` (husky `^9.1.7`): rebar printed `hooks-executable ✗ … .husky/pre-commit — fix with: git update-index --chmod=+x`, about a hook that runs there on every commit, and following the advice would have changed nothing. Read from the published `husky@9.1.7` tarball: `index.js` runs `git config core.hooksPath .husky/_`, writes `.husky/_/<hook>` ITSELF with `mode: 0o755`, copies its `husky` script to `.husky/_/h`, and writes `.husky/_/.gitignore` as `*` so none of that is committed; `.husky/_/h` ends with `sh -e "$s" "$@"`, where `$s` is the committed `.husky/<hook>`. It is sourced through an explicit interpreter, so the execute bit on the committed file decides nothing, and husky 9 hooks carry no shebang by design. THE VERSION IS THE WHOLE OF THE DIFFERENCE, and it is what the two sides here differ in: `husky@8.0.3` (`lib/index.js`, read the same way) runs `git config core.hooksPath <dir>` with `<dir>` being `.husky` ITSELF, the committed directory — there git executes the committed file directly and a 100644 hook is ignored on Linux exactly as the rule says. The two trees are the same bytes, the same 100644 mode and the same `.husky/pre-commit`; only the declared major changes. Whoever exempts on the PATH — `.husky/` and husky in the manifest, with no version — turns the fail side green and stops accusing every husky 8 repository there is.

regras.titulo: the gate was not left with an install placeholder

porque.texto: FINDING FROM USING THE GENERATOR FOR REAL, 02/09. The owner asked for a real site, and generating one exposed this: the CONTENT placeholder is inert and loud — the build fails while a `TROQUE-…` is left. The GATE placeholder was inert and MUTE.

The git identity on this machine is local to the rebar repository, not global. The generator found none, wrote `DONO NÃO CONFIGURADO` in NOTICE, README and `.rebar-coauthors`, and rebar-check gave 13 of 13, exit 0 on top of that.

The worst of the three is `.rebar-coauthors`: it becomes the allowlist of who may sign a commit, with an `@exemplo.invalido` e-mail inside. Nobody matches that e-mail, so the `coautoria-ia` rule starts failing every commit — or, depending on how it is read, none. A gate installed with a placeholder is a gate people learn to switch off in the first week.

The Portuguese in MARCA is a CONTRACT with the generator, not prose: `new/index.mjs` writes `DONO NÃO CONFIGURADO` and `configure-git-user-email@exemplo.invalido`, and the site templates write `TROQUE-…`. Translating it makes the gate stop seeing them.

provas.porque: Found with the real generator on 02/09, asked for by the owner. The CONTENT placeholder is inert and loud: the build fails while a TROQUE- is left — the token stays Portuguese because it is the literal `new/site/aplicar.mjs` writes. The GATE placeholder was inert and MUTE — the generator did not find the git identity, wrote "DONO NÃO CONFIGURADO" (also a literal, written by `new/index.mjs`) in NOTICE, README and .rebar-coauthors, and rebar-check gave 13 of 13, exit 0 on top of that. The worst one is .rebar-coauthors: it is the allowlist of who may sign a commit, and with an @exemplo.invalido e-mail inside it the co-authorship rule stops holding. A gate installed with a placeholder is a gate people learn to switch off in the first week.

regras.titulo: co-authorship only by humans from the allowlist

porque.texto: Maintenance automation leaves before any count, so that it appears neither in the verdict nor in the printed NUMBER — see AUTOMACAO_NAO_IA. Zero co-authorship trailers is the only verdict that does NOT depend on knowing who is AI and who is a person: there is no co-author at all, therefore no AI co-author. It holds with and without an allowlist, and it is the case of this repository's 11 commits. It leaves before everything else so the N/A branch below never swallows a repository that is genuinely clean. Without an allowlist only ENUMERATION is left, and enumeration is the form this fix exists to abandon: measured on 2026-08-30, the list of 9 agents let Windsurf, ChatGPT, Cody, Codeium, Amazon Q and Tabnine through in one go. Here it survives for a narrow reason: rebar-check runs against a THIRD PARTY's repository, which does not have rebar's allowlist, and turning the rule off there would trade a leaky gate for no gate at all.

What changes is what enumeration has the right to ASSERT. Found a known agent, it fails — enumeration proves presence. Found none, it does NOT pass: it becomes N/A saying there is a co-author that cannot be classified. Enumeration does not prove absence, and a "✓" there would be the checker asserting what it does not know. Same discipline as the `na()` at the top of this file: what cannot be decided leaves the denominator, with the reason printed.

provas.porque: Both trees have the SAME file: only the history changes, so the proof measures exactly what the rule reads. The fail side uses the Cursor trailer in lower case (`Co-authored-by:`) because the naive regex looks only for `Claude` with a capital C and covers 15% of the measured problem; the pass side has a commit that CITES Claude and Copilot in the body, which is the false positive that shows up the moment somebody removes the `^` or the `/m` from the regex and it starts matching the bare word in the middle of the text.

Locks the POLICY INVERSION. Both sides have the SAME tree, including the same `.rebar-coauthors` with a single human — only the history changes. The `fail` side uses `Co-authored-by: Windsurf <agent@windsurf.com>`, chosen because Windsurf was NOT in the list of 9 agents the rule enumerated: measured on 2026-08-30, in a repository assembled in tmpdir, Windsurf, ChatGPT, Cody, Codeium, Amazon Q and Tabnine entered the history with a trailer that `git log --format=%(trailers)` recognized and the rule accused 1 of 9 commits while 8 of them had a trailer. Whoever reintroduces enumeration in place of the allowlist turns this side green, and the proof accuses. The `pass` side uses the e-mail that IS in the allowlist and proves the other half: an allowlist that bars everybody is not an allowlist, it is a veto.

The agent list ended in a loose `\[bot\]`, and that wildcard asserted something false: that every GitHub App signing a trailer is an AI agent. Measured on 2026-08-30: `repo-d` was accused of "1 of 25 commits with AI co-authorship" and the ONLY trailer in the whole history is `dependabot[bot]`; in `openkartline` the wildcard inflated the accusation from 2 to 6, because 4 of the 6 were dependabot. A dependency bumper does not write code from a prompt — it is the same judgment the `identidade-git` rule already makes with `EH_BOT`. Both sides have the SAME dependabot commit; the `fail` side adds ONE commit with AI-agent co-authorship, and that is the only difference. Whoever gives the wildcard back turns the `pass` side red; whoever removes the whole enumeration turns `fail` green.

The THIRD-PARTY repository branch, which has no `.rebar-coauthors` — neither side has the file. There all that is left is enumerating agents, and enumeration only proves PRESENCE. The `fail` side has an agent from the list and keeps failing, so the fall back to plan B did not unarm the rule. The `pass` side has a co-author the list does not know and therefore declares `na`: a `✓` there would be the checker asserting "there is no AI" with no way to know, which is exactly the assertion the six agents of the 2026-08-30 attack disproved. A third-party repository with NO trailer at all passes by another path — the absence of a co-author is proof of the absence of an AI co-author — and that is the `coautoria-ia` case with no variant.

A freshly initialized repository, with the tree in the index and no commit, is a legitimate state — and it makes `git log` exit 128. The N/A branch exists because the alternative is the `catch` that swallowed the error and returned an empty string, and an empty string has no co-authorship trailer: the repository with no history PASSED a rule about history. A crash becoming a pass is the same class of defect that `git()` documents. The `pass` side declares `"commits": []` and has to come out N/A; the `fail` side has the trailer and keeps failing, so the guard did not switch the rule off.

regras.titulo: consistent author identity

porque.texto: COUNTING COMBINATIONS WAS THE DEFECT. Two humans in a repository are two combinations, and the rule failed — a false positive against a team, which is the thing this house avoids most: a wrong automatic rule costs more than a missing rule. What follows separates what the ruler PROVES from what it merely suspects.
The GitHub login written INSIDE the address, or null.

`<id>+<login>@users.noreply.github.com` is issued by the platform for one account, so the login in it is not a nickname somebody chose to type — it is the account's own identifier, in the address itself.

ONE ADDRESS, ITS DISPLAY NAME AND ITS OWN LOGIN, IS ONE PERSON — and this was measured on this repository on 2026-09-08, caused by GitHub's own squash button. Thirty-six commits say `Naves <58537948+Navesz@users.noreply.github.com>`; the squash merge of a pull request wrote `Navesz` in the name, because the platform attributes a squash with the LOGIN and not with the display name.

The old branch read that as one e-mail with two names and failed the repository. It is not a drift anybody can fix: rewriting it means force-pushing the default branch past a ruleset that blocks exactly that, and the next squash writes it again. A rule that fails on the merge button of the forge it audits is a rule people switch off — and the reasoning that clears it is already in this file, three paragraphs down: the login proves the account.

What it does NOT clear: the same address with two names that are not its login, which stays a failure. And it can never clear a personal address, because only the noreply form carries a login at all. 1 · COLLISION — the deterministic core. One name with two e-mails, or one e-mail with two names, is not "two people": it is an inconsistent identity, which is the name of the rule. It is the case measured in the forensics — the same person now as `Ana Souza <…noreply>`, now as `ana <ana@empresa.com.br>`, and `git shortlog` counting two. 1b · THE GITHUB LOGIN SHOWING UP TWICE. This is the case collision does not catch and the forensics measured: `Ana Souza <12345+ana@users.noreply.github.com>` and `ana <ana@empresa.com.br>` are the same person, and name and e-mail differ in both.

The link is written in the address. The format is `<id>+<login>@users.noreply.github.com`, so the login is `ana` — a platform identifier, not an invented nickname. When it reappears as the NAME of another identity or as the local part of its e-mail, it is the same person with two identities, and the effect is what the rule exists to prevent: the personal e-mail enters the public history and `git shortlog` counts two people where there is one. THE HARM IS THE SECOND ADDRESS, NOT THE SECOND NAME. What this branch exists to catch is one person appearing under two ADDRESSES, one of them personal, so the private e-mail lands in the public history and `git shortlog` counts two people. When both identities carry the SAME noreply address, none of that happened: nothing leaked, and the login showing up as a display name is what GitHub's squash button writes. Failing it here would be the same false positive the collision branch above just stopped producing, arriving one branch later — and the message would assert a personal e-mail that is demonstrably not there. 2 · NO COLLISION, BUT THE REPOSITORY ALREADY DECLARED WHO IS HUMAN. The list is the SAME one the co-authorship rule uses, on purpose: the question is the same — "who is human on this project?" — and two lists diverge. Its header already says that whoever answers for the commit is the owner of the e-mail. 3 · NO COLLISION AND NO LIST. The ruler has no way of knowing whether these are N people or one person with N identities, and inventing an answer is what it used to do. `na` leaves the denominator with the reason in plain sight: a declared non-measurement is worth more than a guess, and the reason points at the fix.

provas.porque: The real failure is the same person committing now as `Ana Souza <...@users.noreply.github.com>`, now as `ana <ana@empresa.com.br>`: the public history starts carrying the personal e-mail and `git shortlog` counts two people where there is one. The pass side has TWO commits with the identical identity, so a rule that counted commits instead of distinct name/e-mail combinations would fail there and the proof would accuse.

Measured on the rebar repository itself on 2026-09-08. Thirty-six commits carried `Naves <58537948+Navesz@users.noreply.github.com>`; the squash merge of pull request #26 wrote `Navesz` -- the LOGIN -- in the author name, because that is how GitHub attributes a squash. The rule read one e-mail with two names and failed the repository, and the drift is unfixable by design: rewriting it means force-pushing the default branch past a ruleset that exists to block exactly that, and the next squash writes it again. A rule that fails on the merge button of the forge it audits is a rule people switch off. The pass side is that exact shape -- one address, its display name, and its own login, which the address itself proves is one account. The fail side is the SAME address with a second name that is NOT its login, which is the drift the rule exists to catch and which this exemption must not swallow. Without the fail side, an exemption keyed on `p.nome === login` could be widened to `any second name` and nothing would notice.

The two N/A branches of the rule, one per folder. `pass/` declares `"commits": []`: with no history there is no identity to compare, and the version that swallowed the `git log` error made this repository PASS on a rule about authorship. `fail/` has a single commit, from dependabot: a bot commits, and committing does not make it an inconsistent identity of the owner. This second branch has a measured price — without the bot list, the merge commit GitHub creates at refs/pull/N/merge counted as a second person AND as an exposed personal e-mail, two false positives at once, and EVERY pull request was born failed.

P2 #5 of the external audit. The rule counted distinct name/e-mail combinations among non-bot authors and failed with more than one -- so two people in a repository failed, which is a false positive against a team, and a wrong automatic rule costs more than a missing rule. The pass side has TWO real humans: different names, different e-mails, no login repeating, and both declared in `.rebar-coauthors`. Nothing there is identity inconsistency. The fail side has the SAME two people plus a third identity nobody declared -- which is what the list exists to catch, and the fix is one line. Both sides carry the tracked allowlist, otherwise the verdict would be `na` on both and the case would prove nothing. `na` stays as it is: it is the state value prove.mjs matches on (prove.mjs:198-200), not prose.

regras.titulo: components/ui/ accompanied by components.json

porque.texto: The BASE of a UI folder is the directory that contains `components/`: `apps/web/src/components/ui/botao.tsx` has base `apps/web/src/`. That is where the search for the defense climbs from.

provas.porque: The real failure is the `components/ui/` folder made by hand to LOOK like shadcn without ever having gone through the CLI: with no `components.json`, `npx shadcn add` does not know where to write, the aliases do not exist and the next person thinks they can update a component nobody generates. Both trees have the same `components/ui/botao.tsx`; only the `components.json` changes, so if the rule stops looking at it the fail side exits 0 and the proof accuses.

The false-positive class "defect searched recursively, defense searched only at the root". The rule swept `components/ui/` at any depth and checked `components.json` only in `r.dir`: measured, prumo, repo-d and repo-l were the three accused of imitating the convention while all three had the file tracked in a subfolder (apps/web/, apps/web/, web/). Five of the twelve audited repositories are monorepos, and the accusation landed precisely on them. The two trees are identical except for `apps/web/components.json`. The `apps/loja/components.json` is on BOTH sides on purpose: it makes the proof immune to the lazy fix — swapping "only at the root" for "exists anywhere" would make the `fail` side exit 0, because a sibling package's `components.json` would start defending `apps/web/`. Only proximity matching, walking up the tree from the UI folder, makes both sides come out right.

regras.titulo: no Brazilian phone number in the code

porque.texto: PROMOTED FROM HEURISTIC TO DETERMINISTIC, and the number that decided it is here.

§12.3 of the plan settled the decision that gives this its teeth: phone, CNPJ and address are validated CONTENT, not code and not an environment variable. And the cost of the mistake is documented in client-a itself: `client-a#1` tried to move the number into an env var and the owner stopped the PR, because the build passes and the `wa.me` ships with no recipient. Deterministic is what makes the decision hold.

The pattern was TIGHTENED along with the promotion, and that is the expensive half. The old `\(?\d{2}\)?\s?9\d{4}-?\d{4}` accepted ELEVEN DIGITS IN A ROW with no punctuation at all, with a `9` in the third place: a product EAN-13 (`7891234599999`) matched. Acceptable in a heuristic that only informs; unacceptable in a rule that fails merges. Now only what carries a MARK of a Brazilian phone counts — a `wa.me` link, country code 55, or the DDD punctuation. The same client-a is still caught (`55` + `24` + `9` + eight digits) and the other 416 files stay clean: the tightening did not cost a single true positive.

The patterns below describe the shape of a BRAZILIAN phone number — the `wa.me` link, the 55 country code, the DDD in parentheses. They are the subject of the rule, not prose, and there is nothing in them to translate. Comments out: see the `semComentario` note. What §12.3 forbids is the number the program USES — the one that ships in the `wa.me` and in the `tel:` —, and that one lives in executed code, not in a footnote. ELEVEN RAW DIGITS count ONLY when the file assembles a `wa.me` or a `tel:`. It is the fix for a regression the tightening above caused and the audit caught: the SAME client-a mobile written without the country code, in the same file, assembling the same link, passed clean. Context is what separates a phone from a barcode: an EAN-13 does not become a WhatsApp link, and that is why the raw digits only count accompanied.

provas.porque: §12.3 of the plan settled that a phone number is validated CONTENT, not code and not an environment variable, and the cost of getting it wrong is documented in client-a itself: PR `client-a#1` tried to move the number into an env var and the owner stopped the PR, because the build passes, the deploy goes up and `wa.me` generates a link with no recipient. The rule became deterministic with one true and zero false positives across 417 measured code files. Both sides have the SAME number written the SAME way: on the `pass` side it is in a COMMENT and on `fail` in a constant the program uses. A comment does not go up in `wa.me`, and a ruler that accused comments would accuse the very note that explains it — which is what happened in this repository while this rule was being written.

P2 of the external audit, and the fix already existed in another module without having been propagated. `core.quotePath` is true by default on EVERY system, so `git ls-files` without `-z` returns `configuração.mjs` -- the fixture file name stays Portuguese, it is the accent that is being tested -- as `"configura\\303\\247\\303\\243o.mjs"`, quoted and escaped. `lerRepo` passed that quoting along as if it were a file name, `readFileSync` failed, and the failure was swallowed: the file left the scoreboard without having been read. The old pattern accepted ELEVEN DIGITS IN A ROW with no punctuation at all, as long as there was a `9` in the third position — and a product EAN-13 barcode matches that. porque.texto: WHY IT STAYS A HEURISTIC, with the number in hand.

After the two fixes below the rule went from 12 accused files in 7 repositories to 6 files in 5, and the 6 are literally true — none is a false positive. Separating the two requires knowing the deploy origin, and the checker does not know it. Blocking merges at 2-of-6 precision on the defect the rule names is punishing correct behavior — and a rule that punishes correct behavior teaches people to turn the whole output off.
FIX 1 — the env-fallback pattern, which is the RIGHT pattern.

`process.env.X ?? 'https://…'` is exactly what you want a person to write: an environment variable with a sensible default. Measured: `decima-edicoes/app/lib/site.ts:5` accused over `process.env.NEXT_PUBLIC_SITE_URL ?? 'https://navesz.github.io/decima-edicoes'`, and `client-b` accused TWICE over the same shape (`scripts/check-access.js:3` and `src/lib/accessControl.ts:6`). The fallback is erased from the text BEFORE the search, and not the whole file: a file can have the right pattern on one line and the raw address on another, and absolving the file because of the good line would trade this false positive for a false negative. FIX 2 — an address only counts when it is used AS an address.

The literal has to OPEN a string and come right after a request call or an address name. Measured, three accusations fell and none of the three held up once the file was opened: openkartline/apps/web/src/App.tsx:521 — `href="https://github.com/…"`, a footer link to the repository itself. A link is a link. prumo/…/migrations/20260825_0003_credentials.ts — twenty `doc: 'https://docs.fal.ai'` fields, a documentation catalog seeded into a table. It is DATA, and a table is the right place for data. prumo/…/collectors/index.ts:76 — the address inside the `User-Agent` string. It opens no string, so it never even gets tested. Portuguese in the list for the same reason as `NOMES_TYPECHECK` and `NOME_TESTE`, and it must NOT be translated: a ruler that only recognizes English variable names is blind to the repository it exists to measure. `origem`, `endereco` and `servidor` are what a project from here writes where `decima-edicoes` wrote `origin`. 60 characters are enough for the roomiest `const LONG_NAME =` and keep a neighboring line from lending its verdict to the next one.
