Until 2026-09-07 this rule pulled the comments out with the same naive pair that `semComentario` stopped being — and it had the same defect, measured here: a block-opener inside a string literal in `new/gate/aplicar.mjs` opened a bogus comment and dragged `destino: 'preservado', porque:` into the text about to be judged. Two extractions of one concept are two sources to diverge, and these did.

A span between backticks is CODE QUOTED, not prose, and leaves before the language test. An identifier in English inside a Portuguese comment is not a language switch, it is the name of the thing — nobody translates `User-Agent`, `<input type="file">` or `cat-file --batch`.

Measured on 2026-08-31 on the rebar mirror with `new/` tracked: the `en` count fell from 3 to 0, and those 3 were exactly these three files, all with Portuguese prose — `index.mjs`, `scan-secret.mjs` and `new/index.mjs`. With min(pt,en) >= 3 as the floor, those three carried the whole accusation.

A span between QUOTES leaves for the same reason, and the reason is stronger: quoted speech is not the writer's prose, and translating what somebody said is rewriting it, not translating. This repository is full of the owner's words kept verbatim with the English in brackets after them, and of sample strings measured in Brazilian repositories — the measurement IS the Portuguese. Measured on 2026-09-07, after the translation: 9 of the 11 files the rule was accusing were quotation only. Without this the rule fails on the very repository it is the reference for, which is how the naive colour rule died.

provas.porque: It was the last of the 21 rules with no case, and a rule with no case is a rule nobody can refactor safely. The real failure is the repository that switches language halfway through: `prumo`, measured on 2026-08-30, has 24 files with Portuguese comments and 47 in English, and the next person writes in the language of the file they opened first. The floor is `min(pt, en) >= 3` on purpose — one stray English line in a Portuguese repository is a quotation, not a language switch — and the two sides exist to lock that floor from both directions: `pass` has FOUR files in Portuguese and zero in English, `fail` has the same four plus THREE in English, exactly the floor. Whoever lowers the floor to 1 leaves `pass` green and is not caught; whoever raises it to 4 turns `fail` green and is. The Portuguese in both trees is fixture, not prose: it is what the rule's PT stopword regex looks for, and translating it blinds the rule.

A regra ja tirava trecho entre crases, com o argumento de que "codigo citado nao e prosa" -- um `User-Agent` dentro de um comentario em portugues nao e troca de idioma, e o nome da coisa. Trecho entre ASPAS sai pelo mesmo argumento, e ele e mais forte: fala citada nao e a prosa de quem escreve, e traduzi-la e reescrever o que a pessoa disse. Medido no proprio rebar em 2026-09-07, depois de a arvore ir para o ingles: a regra acusava 11 arquivos, e 9 deles eram SO citacao -- fala do dono preservada com a traducao entre colchetes, e amostras de texto medidas em repositorios brasileiros, onde o portugues E a medicao. Sem esta correcao a regra reprova o repositorio que e a referencia dela, que e exatamente como a versao ingenua da regra de cor literal morreu. O lado aprovar tem tres arquivos cujo unico portugues esta entre aspas; o lado reprovar tem os mesmos tres com a prosa em volta em portugues de verdade. Quem tirar o `.replace` das aspas faz o lado aprovar ficar vermelho.

regras.titulo: no .env tracked by git

porque.texto: The most common class in the whole inventory: a versioned secret shows up in 7 of the 16 videos. This is its cheapest slice — a `git ls-files`.

It is NOT the secret scanner, which already exists in `tooling/secret/`. That one looks at the staged CONTENT; this one looks at the tracked NAME. They are different findings: a `.env` can be tracked and empty today and get the key tomorrow with nobody noticing, because the file already went through review.

False positive predicted and excluded: `.env.example`, `.env.sample`, `.env.template`, `.env.dist` and `.env.exemplo` are the FIX for this flaw, not the flaw. A repository that documents its variables in a tracked `.env.example` is doing the right thing.
N5 and not N1 because the fix after the commit is not deleting the file: it is rotating the credential. The place to block is before the commit exists.

provas.porque: A versioned secret is the most common class in the inventory: 7 of the 16 videos. This is the cheapest slice of it, one `git ls-files`. The fail side has a tracked `.env`; the pass side has `.env.example` AND `.env.sample` tracked, which are the FIX for the failure and not the failure -- documenting the variables without the values is exactly what is asked for. Whoever removes the example exclusion makes the pass side go red; whoever swaps the check for "a .env exists on disk" makes the fail side go green, because a `.env` ignored by git is no finding at all. The fail `.env` is written only to the index of the assembled repository (`gerados`), never as a file under this folder: a `.env` is also a file agent-config-exec reads, and a tracked one here would put a real agent config file inside rebar's own tree.

regras.titulo: no framework protection turned off by a literal

porque.texto: The cheapest gap the inventory audit found, and it was not even in the inventory: no video showed it, but it is the most deterministic pattern there is in a repository built with AI.

Every literal in this list is a HUMAN DECISION recorded on one line — somebody turned a protection off so the demo would stop erroring, and never turned it back on. There is no dataflow, no schema, no proof of absence: the literal is there or it is not. That is why the false positive tends to zero and the finding explains itself.
It brings CSRF (CWE-352, third in the CWE Top 25) into the module, which would otherwise be left with no rule at all.

FALSE POSITIVE PREDICTED AND HANDLED: the very file that documents these patterns — this one — would match every one of them. That is what `semComentarioNemImport` solves (I7), and it is the reason the body is read without comments.

Source already comes with the text; config and workflow need a read. THE MATCHED TEXT, and not a copy of it typed into the table. The output reads as before -- `rejectUnauthorized: false — TLS without ...` -- except that the literal is now what IS in the audited file, with the spacing it really has. DEBUG on only counts alongside an open host: `DEBUG = True` by itself is the development default, and flagging it paints every settings.py.

explicacoes: TLS without verifying the certificate
turns TLS off for the whole process
requests without verifying the certificate
route with no CSRF protection
CSRF turned off
helmet without a CSP
download without checking the cert

provas.porque: The cheapest gap the inventory audit found, and it did not come from any video: it is the most deterministic pattern there is in a repository built with AI. Each literal is a human decision recorded on one line -- somebody switched the protection off so the demo would stop erroring and never switched it back on. The pass side carries the false positive that takes down a naive detector: the SAME literal written inside a comment, documenting why it must NOT be used. Without `semComentarioNemImport` the pass side goes red, and this module's own rules file would accuse itself.

P2 #4 of the external audit, and the only case in this module that is not about the rule: it is about what the rule CAN SEE. `semComentarioNemImport` was two regex substitutions with no notion of a string, so a block opener INSIDE A STRING opened a comment that only closed at the file's next block closer -- and erased everything in between. Measured across rebar's 139 code files: 9 had code outside the examination, the worst with 1,181 tokens. Here the fail side has `rejectUnauthorized: false` between a string with a block opener and the JSDoc that closes it; with the old remover that side goes GREEN, which is a false negative, the worst outcome for a ruler. The pass side has the SAME string and the SAME JSDoc, and no disabled defense: it is the one that guarantees the fix did not turn into accusing a string with a slash and an asterisk inside.

regras.titulo: password never compared in plain text nor by a fast hash

porque.texto: Third most common class in the inventory — 4 of the 16 videos. Chosen ahead of `mass-assignment`, which shows up in 5, for a cost reason: mass assignment only decides severity by reading the privileged column of the schema, which demands a `schema.prisma` or SQL parser. This one is textual all the way through.
TWO SIGNALS, and both need bilingual vocabulary:

(a) direct comparison — `u.password === req.body.password`, or the same with `senha`. If the comparison is `===`, it never went through a KDF: bcrypt, argon2 and scrypt return a hash with the salt embedded and demand `compare`.
(b) fast hash on an authentication path — `createHash('sha256')`, `md5`, `sha1`. Fast is the defect: what protects a password is being slow.

FALSE POSITIVE PREDICTED AND EXCLUDED: LEGITIMATE PRE-HASH. `bcrypt` silently truncates at 72 bytes, and the recommended defense is to feed a sha256 of the password into bcrypt. A file that does `bcrypt.hash(sha256(senha))` is RIGHT, and flagging it would punish whoever knows the problem. That is why signal (b) only counts where there is no slow primitive in the same file.

BILINGUAL vocabulary. See the note at the top: the English-only list is blind in exactly the repositories this module exists to audit. `senha` stays in Portuguese because it is what the rule LOOKS FOR inside third-party Brazilian code — translating it blinds the detector.

`rebar-segredo-ok:` is not prose either: it is the escape token `tooling/secret/scan-secret.mjs` matches, and renaming it voids every escape already written in the audited repositories. Only the justification after the colon is English — the token demands a reason that starts with a character neither whitespace nor default-ignorable, right after the finding and within 256 characters of it, and it gets both.

provas.porque: Third most common class, 4 of the 16 videos, and chosen ahead of mass assignment (which shows up in 5) on cost: mass assignment only decides severity by reading the privileged column of the schema, and that requires a parser. This one is textual all the way through. The fail side compares with `===`, which proves there was no KDF -- bcrypt and argon2 return a salted hash and require `compare`. The pass side carries the false positive that matters: LEGITIMATE PRE-HASH. bcrypt truncates at 72 bytes without a word, and the recommended defense is to feed it a sha256 of the password. Whoever does that is RIGHT, and accusing them would punish the person who knows the problem -- which is why the fast-hash signal only holds where there is no slow primitive in the same file. The vocabulary is bilingual on both sides: both trees use `senha`, not `password`, because this module audits a Brazilian repository.

regras.titulo: no credential written into a file git tracks

porque.texto: THE MEASUREMENT THAT OPENED THIS RULE. A repository was built with four credentials of real shape — an AWS access key, a GitHub token, an LLM API key, and the assignment of a literal to an `apiKey` constant, which is the exact shape of a live one found in a public repository today. Both rulers were run against it:
rebar-security . 2 of 2, 1 not applicable, EXIT 0 — saw nothing rebar . none of the 23 rules mentions a credential

The detector that catches all four already existed and worked: `tooling/secret/scan-secret.mjs` exited 1 with 4 findings on the same tree. It was simply not a rule of either ruler — it ran only as an internal step of rebar's own gate, and as the pre-commit hook of the generated project.

WHY THAT GAP IS THE WHOLE POINT, AND WHY THE LEVEL IS N4. The hook is N5, and N5 is the level `docs/PLANO.md` describes as the one the agent removes WITH NO DIFF AT ALL: `git commit --no-verify` and the scan never happened. What the generated project's CI runs is `npm run verificar`, `npx rebar .` and `npx rebar-security .` — and until this rule none of the three read a single byte looking for a credential. So a secret committed with `--no-verify` reached main with CI green. The mother rule of the taxonomy says a rule that can go down a level must go down: N4 blocks the merge and survives the flag, and this rule is the same scan standing there.

IT DETECTS NOTHING OF ITS OWN. Every pattern, every placeholder list and the `rebar-segredo-ok:` escape come from the scanner, run as a subprocess — see the note above `VARREDOR`. Derived, never duplicated: a second copy of those patterns would drift from the hook's, and then the commit and the merge would disagree about what a credential is.

ABSENCE OF A TARGET IS `na`; ABSENCE OF INFORMATION IS NOT. A repository where git tracks nothing has no credential to hide, and the class leaves the denominator (I4). A repository where the scanner READ NOTHING it tried to read is a different thing entirely — the measurement failed, and laundering that into `na` is exactly the move that once took a repository from 9 of 10 to 6 of 6. It goes out as a broken ruler. The scanner reports paths relative to the GIT ROOT it discovers from its cwd; `lerRepo` reports them relative to the TARGET. The two coincide only when the target is the root, which is the usual call and not the only one. `--show-prefix` is the translation between the two, and without it a target one folder down would be judged by findings from outside itself, with paths that do not exist in it. PROOF MATERIAL, BY THE MARKER THE TOOLKIT ALREADY USES. This repository tracks case files stuffed with credentials that are fake on purpose, including the `fail/` trees that exist to prove THIS rule fails what it should.

The scanner itself now exempts only VALIDATED roots: a tracked `caso.json` with the schema, under a literal proof root, read from the index under `--staged` (HOLE 9 of its header). `r.ignorados.raizesDeProva` is the same validation done by `semFixtures`. So "a `mkdir` plus an empty object does not hide a key" is now true of BOTH — and it was false until that change: on the previous scanner, an empty untracked caso.json made this rule pass (measured, and locked by the `hardcoded-secret__marker-outside-root` case).

WHAT THIS FILTER IS, measured and not assumed: an EXEMPTION, not a lock. It can only remove findings, and at the git root it is a no-op — with it deleted, this rule still passou on rebar, because the scanner already dropped every proof-fixture finding. It changes a verdict only when the target is NOT the git root (rebar vendored under a subfolder, say): the scanner's roots are relative to the git root, `lerRepo`'s to the target.

`.rebarignore` is deliberately NOT honoured. It is a declared bypass for vendor and generated material, and style debt is not a credential: one committed under an ignored prefix leaks in the clone exactly like any other. The scanner refuses folder exclusions for the same reason. Location and rule NAME, never the matched text. The scanner already redacts what it prints because its output goes to a CI log; this one goes to a CI log too, and into `--json`, and the position is enough to find the line without carrying the credential one hop further. Passed, with a hole named. There is no fourth state and there should not be one, but "I scanned everything" and "I did not read these N" are two different claims and the rule was only able to make the first.

provas.porque: The measurement that opened the rule: a repository with four credentials of real shape -- an AWS access key, a GitHub token, an LLM API key and a literal assigned to `apiKey` -- came out of `rebar-security .` as "2 of 2, 1 not applicable, EXIT 0" and out of `rebar .` with none of the 23 rules mentioning a credential, while `tooling/secret/scan-secret.mjs` exited 1 with all four on the same tree. The detector existed and was a rule of no ruler: it ran only in the pre-commit hook, which is N5 and disappears with `git commit --no-verify` leaving no diff. The fail side is that tree. The pass side carries six NAMED false positives, and each one locks a different piece of the scanner's defense: the documentation line that quotes a vendor prefix (the single false positive in 44 attack cases), a value that comes from `process.env`, a `key` with no qualifier, a connection string to localhost, the written `rebar-segredo-ok:` escape, and the `.env.example` placeholder in the unquoted form. Whoever makes this rule read the code WITHOUT comments -- and the temptation is real, because every other rule in this module reads that way -- kills the escape hatch already written into the audited repositories and the pass side goes red. Whoever drops the proof-root filter keeps both sides green and turns rebar's own 345 case files into an accusation, which is why `security-self` is the other half of this proof.

The variant isolates ONE path, because a side satisfied by several paths at once proves none of them: the sibling case fails through four shapes together, and a rule narrowed to vendor-prefix findings only (`AKIA`, `ghp_`, `sk-`) would keep it red with this shape already invisible. This shape has no vendor prefix at all -- what denounces it is the identifier NAME plus the shape of the value -- and it is the exact one living in the main branch of a public repository today. The pass side is the same file with the same identifier in the same URL, fixed by reading `process.env`: a rule that decided by the name alone would fail the fix too, and failing the fix is worse than having no rule, because it teaches people to switch checking off.

Until 2026-09-13 the secret scanner exempted every file below ANY caso.json on disk, in any ancestor folder, even under --staged: an empty, untracked caso.json hidden by .git/info/exclude, or a directory named caso.json, took every finding below it out of the scan in both modes, and hardcoded-secret passed with it. The fail side is a schema-valid src/caso.json OUTSIDE the two literal proof roots, beside one vendor-shaped value (the same synthetic literal the sibling case already commits): a scanner that goes back to 'any ancestor caso.json' turns it green. The pass side is the same marker beside a value read from process.env, so a rule that failed any tree holding a caso.json goes red. Every file here is tracked on disk and none comes from gerados: tracked mode reads the disk, so an index-only fixture would not be read at all and the fail side would come out passed with a coverage note, the wrong verdict.

regras.titulo: no known hidden-Unicode signature in tracked text, file names or commit messages

porque.texto: A model reads code points and a pull request shows glyphs. The Default_Ignorable_Code_Point set (4174 code points in UCD 17.0.0) is the part of Unicode a renderer may draw as nothing, so a line of an agent instruction file can carry a sentence no reviewer sees: tag characters spell ASCII one for one, bidi overrides reorder what the reviewer reads (Trojan Source, CVE-2021-42574), a Hangul filler is a valid identifier that looks empty, and the GlassWorm loader hid in runs of variation selectors.

It reads what git will hand out, not the disk: stage-0 index blobs decoded by their byte order mark, every tracked path and symlink target as a name, every commit message reachable from HEAD, and a second pass over the escapes JSON, YAML and TOML decode by themselves. No proof root, template root or `.rebarignore` hides anything from it.

The exemptions exist because a measurement demanded each one: RGI emoji sequences (rebar's own docs carry 25 warning signs with a presentation selector), script joiners in the scripts that write words with them, a joiner right after a virama on a letter of its script outside code (the Unicode security profile allows that context, and legacy Malayalam and Bengali end words with it), right-to-left marks on lines that are already right-to-left. Agent files and names keep only the joiner between two letters of one script, the Indic conjunct joiners around a virama, and the lone mark on a right-to-left line, which Persian, Arabic and the Indic scripts need. What is left in a repository goes into `.rebar-injection-allowlist` by blob id or commit id.

N4 for the reason hardcoded-secret gives: a hook is removed with no diff, and CI on the merge is the level that survives it. A pass means no known signature matched, never that the repository is free of prompt injection.

provas.porque: The shape the rule exists for: tag characters spell ASCII one for one and render as nothing, so a line of an agent file carries text no reviewer sees. The fail side is AGENTS.md with a run of 12 tag code points after a visible sentence (meaningless letters, no payload). The pass side is the same file with every emoji construct that also uses invisible code points legitimately: a family ZWJ sequence, the Scotland subdivision flag (the only tag sequences Unicode ships), a warning sign with its emoji selector, and keycap one. Loosen the flag exception to "black flag, any tags, cancel tag" and nothing changes here, but drop it or drop the ZWJ or selector exceptions and the pass side goes red; stop reading tags as hidden and the fail side goes green.

Commit messages reach agents through git log and PR tooling, and rebar-check trims them (a trailing U+FEFF was measured gone), so this rule reads history raw. The fail side has one commit whose message carries U+200B inside a word, committed verbatim from bytes. The pass side has the same tree and two honest messages that carry invisibles by accident: one opens with the UTF-8 byte-order mark Windows PowerShell 5.1 writes and `git commit -F` keeps, which is consumed like a file's BOM; the other is a Dependabot body where GitHub put U+200B between '@' and a login so nobody gets pinged. Stop reading commits, or read them through a trimming helper, and the fail side goes green; drop either exemption and the pass side goes red.

The not-applicable branch: a repository whose index is empty and whose history has no commit has nothing this rule could read, and silence by absence must not become passed (invariant I4). Both sides are that repository, with no generated entry and no commit, and both must say na; the rule has one such branch, so the two sides pin it twice rather than proving two branches. Return null instead of na there and both sides diverge.

A path is attacker text too: an agent opens docs/notes.md and gets a different file whose name holds U+200B, and every tool that prints the name prints the invisible along with it. The fail side tracks docs/no<U+200B>tes.md, written only to the index; the pass side tracks docs/notacoes.md spelled with c-cedilla and o-tilde, which proves the name scan is about ignorable code points and not about non-ASCII. Stop scanning names and the fail side goes green; flag any non-ASCII name and the pass side goes red.

U+3164 HANGUL FILLER is a valid JavaScript identifier character that renders as blank, so two identifiers that look identical in review are different bindings. The fail side is src/a.mjs whose identifier carries one U+3164 in the middle; the pass side is the same line without it. Code files get the single-character-literal concession, and this case pins that the concession stops at literals: widen it to any code context and the fail side goes green.

A JSON file can be pure ASCII on disk and hold an invisible after parsing: a unicode escape decodes to the real code point, which is what every client reading the value gets. The fail side is config/x.json whose string value ends in an escaped U+200B; the pass side escapes a visible e-acute the same way, so the case pins that the escape pass judges the decoded code point and not the mere presence of an escape. Scan only raw text and the fail side goes green; flag every escape and the pass side goes red.

Khmer writes no spaces between words and marks a word boundary with U+200B, the script's normal practice: date-fns' km locale carries 12 of them. The pass side is docs/km.md with one U+200B between two Khmer words. The fail side is the same line in AGENTS.md, where no script exemption applies because an agent obeys the file. Remove the Khmer boundary exemption and the pass side goes red; extend it to agent files and the fail side goes green.

U+200F RIGHT-TO-LEFT MARK is ordinary punctuation inside Arabic or Hebrew text, where it fixes the order of numbers and Latin runs, and a hidden carrier anywhere else. Both sides are docs/ar.md with one RLM before a year; on the pass side the line is Arabic, on the fail side the same line has no right-to-left letter. Remove the line-context exception and the pass side goes red; exempt the mark everywhere and the fail side goes green.

A byte order mark is legitimate once, at byte 0, and nowhere else. Measured: TextDecoder with its default ignoreBOM:false silently removes a second one, so a decoder that strips "the BOM" twice hides a U+FEFF from the rule. The fail side is docs/notes.md starting with two UTF-8 BOMs; the pass side starts with one. Let the decoder eat the second mark and the fail side goes green; treat the first one as a finding and the pass side goes red.

Agent instruction files and file names are judged in strict mode, and strict mode had dropped the two exemptions Persian and Arabic are written with: a zero-width non-joiner inside a Persian word, and a right-to-left mark that keeps a number in place on an Arabic line. A Persian CLAUDE.md, an Arabic AGENTS.md and a Persian file name all failed on their own words. Strict mode now keeps one joiner with a letter of the same joining script on each side, and one bidi mark on a line that has right-to-left script, and nothing else. The pass side tracks exactly those three. The fail side tracks the same CLAUDE.md with a zero-width space in place of the joiner and the same AGENTS.md with a right-to-left override in place of the mark. Whoever drops the strict exemptions turns the pass side red; whoever applies the prose exemptions to agent files turns the fail side green. Content and the name are base64 because rebar reads its own caso.json raw.

git treats a UTF-16 file as binary (numstat prints a dash, git grep misses it), so a UTF-16 CLAUDE.md is invisible to diff review while the agent decodes it fine. Measured: a naive UTF-8 read of such a file finds 0 of 12 hidden code points and a BOM decode finds all 12. Both sides are CLAUDE.md in UTF-16LE with a byte order mark; the fail side has U+200B inside a word. Decode without the BOM, or skip what git calls binary, and the fail side goes green; read the bytes as UTF-8, find the NUL half of every code unit and call the agent file unreadable, and the pass side goes red.

UTS #39 section 3.1.1.1 (rules A2 and B) and RFC 5892 CONTEXTJ allow a joiner right after a virama that sits on a letter, and Malayalam text written before Unicode 5.1 ends a word with the legacy chillu, consonant plus virama plus ZWJ, before a space. The pass side is docs/ml.md with that word-final chillu in prose, plus an AGENTS.md with the Sinhala conjunct SHA, AL-LAKUNA, ZWJ, RA, II, where a letter of the same script follows the joiner. The fail side is an AGENTS.md whose legacy chillu is followed by a space and a Latin letter. Without the exemption the pass side goes red; extending it to a word-final joiner in agent files turns the fail side green.

regras.titulo: no known terminal-control signature in tracked text

porque.texto: A C0 or C1 control in a tracked text file acts on the terminal that prints it: a colour sequence conceals what follows, a backspace or a bare carriage return overwrites what came before, and `git diff` pages through a pager that passes colour sequences raw. The reviewer reads less than the model that reads the blob.

Measured before the rule existed, over the 744 files tracked by rebar, rebar-site and bookkeep: the only raw control was rebar's own colour helper, 2 bytes on one line. Code keeps a narrower set, because honest sources carry sentinels (a YAML plugin, a PNG magic), and a file whose line endings are all bare carriage returns is a warning, not a finding. In prose and data files a form feed alone on its line (a license page break) and a colour sequence whose parameters all keep text visible (a test snapshot) pass, because neither hides anything; concealing, background and cursor sequences still fail.

JSON and YAML parsers refuse a raw control, so the attack reaches them as the format's own escape. Those escapes go through the same decoder hidden-unicode uses, and fail the same way. Tracked names and commit messages are read too, because `git log` and `ls-files` print them raw.

provas.porque: The signature the rule exists for, measured in the wild: an SGR sequence in a tracked text file. A terminal acts on it, and `git diff` goes through `less -R`, which passes it through raw, so the line after the sequence is concealed from whoever reviews the diff while a model reading the blob gets all of it. The fail side is notes.txt with ESC followed by the conceal code before an ordinary sentence. The pass side is the same kind of file with the two controls every honest text file carries, TAB and CRLF line endings: a rule that failed every C0 code point, or treated CR as a control even before LF, would turn every Windows checkout red and teach people to switch it off.

The one-byte CSI, U+009B, opens a control sequence exactly like ESC plus a bracket, and VTE-based terminals, Kitty and WezTerm accept C1 controls inside UTF-8. A rule looking only at C0 misses it. The fail side is docs/a.md with U+009B encoded as UTF-8 before a colour code. The pass side is the character a cp1252 reader would have meant by that byte, the single right-pointing angle quotation mark, encoded properly: the check is on decoded code points, so the visible character passes and only the control fails.

Code gets a smaller character set, and this case locks both edges of it. Measured in node_modules, honest source carries C0 sentinels (a YAML plugin uses U+0002, U+0018 and U+001F; a PNG magic uses U+001A), and failing them would put every vendored parser in the allowlist. So the pass side is src/a.mjs with U+0002 inside a string. The fail side is the same line with ESC instead, which a code file never needs raw: the escape can always be written as source text, which is how rebar fixed its own colour helper.

In a double-quoted PowerShell string a backtick is the escape character, so a commit message typed as -m "use `actions/checkout`" stores BEL where the Markdown code span began; a real history carries three of them, and a published commit cannot be reworded. A bell, vertical tab or form feed rings or moves the cursor and hides no text, so in a commit message it is a note. A backspace overwrites what the terminal printed, so it still fails. The pass side has one commit with the PowerShell shape (BEL before the letters of two code spans); the fail side has one commit with a backspace. Whoever fails every C0 control in a message turns the pass side red; whoever lets every control in a message through turns the fail side green. Messages are base64 because rebar reads its own caso.json raw.

git calls a blob binary when its first 8000 bytes hold a NUL, and a small compressed or encrypted blob often holds none: 243 random bytes miss one about 39% of the time. Read as text, every stray C0 byte in it was a finding, and an honest repository of extracted firmware failed with 25,972 of them. The pass side is assets/radio.dat, 243 fixed high-entropy bytes behind a zlib header with no 0x00: the window is not UTF-8 and most of it decodes to replacement characters or C0, so it is binary. The fail side is the same bytes under a .txt name, which must be text whatever it holds, so its controls still fail. Drop the entropy test and the pass side goes red; apply it to must-be-text names and the fail side goes green.

A raw 0x9B byte is not UTF-8: it decodes to a replacement character, not to CSI. Failing raw bytes 0x80-0x9F would fail Brazilian docs saved in cp1252, which is why the rule judges decoded code points and a lenient decode is only a nota outside agent files. The pass side is docs/a.md with that raw byte. The fail side is the same bytes in AGENTS.md: an instruction file that is not valid UTF-8 may be read one way by the client and another way by the reviewer, so there it is a reading problem and it fails.

In JSON the raw byte is not the vector, because JSON.parse refuses it. The vector is the format escape: a unicode escape of ESC inside a string is clean text on disk and a real ESC after parsing, in whatever the client prints. The fail side is config.json with that escape in a description. The pass side has the same characters preceded by an escaped backslash, which decodes to a literal backslash and the text after it, not to a control: a rule that ignored backslash parity would fail every regex pattern and Windows path stored in JSON.

A carriage return that is not followed by a line feed sends the terminal back to column 0, and what follows overwrites what came before: the reviewer reads the second half of the line, the model reads both. The class the plan started from allowed CR outright, which is exactly this hole (evasao-adversarial measured it). The fail side is README.md with one bare CR in the middle of a line. The pass side is the same README with CRLF endings: a CR that ends a line is not a control trick, and failing it would fail every file saved on Windows.

git decides binary by a NUL in the first 8000 bytes, prints "Binary files differ" and hides the change from review. If the rule skipped such files the same way, one NUL at the top of AGENTS.md would take the whole instruction file out of every scan. So a NUL in an agent file or in a must-be-text extension fails, and that is the fail side. The pass side is a file of unknown type with a NUL early and a DEL after it: that is binary content, skipped and not judged, which is what keeps images and executables from failing.

GNU license files, Emacs Lisp and Python put a form feed alone on its line as a page break (GNU Coding Standards 5.1, PEP 8), and xterm treats FF like LF: it hides no text. Measured, 90 of 101 form feeds in the licenses and libraries of Git for Windows and Python 3.12 sit alone on their line. The pass side is a COPYING with one on its own LF line and a docs/LICENSE.txt with one on its own CRLF line. The fail side is a README.md with a form feed in the middle of a line. Without the exemption the pass side goes red; exempting every form feed in prose turns the fail side green.

A CLI test snapshot records the colours the program printed, and SGR red, green, bold and dim leave every word visible. SGR 8 is Invisible in the xterm control sequences, and git pages diffs through less -R, which passes SGR raw, so a reviewer of the snapshot sees nothing where a model reads an instruction. The exemption reads the sequence, never the path. The pass side is src/__snapshots__/cli.test.js.snap with red, dim, bold and green sequences; the fail side is the same file where one sequence conceals a phrase. Without the exemption the pass side goes red; accepting every SGR parameter, or exempting the __snapshots__ folder, turns the fail side green.

YAML decodes escapes only inside double-quoted scalars, and its short escape for ESC is two characters that look like nothing on disk. The fail side is config/a.yml with that escape in a double-quoted value, which js-yaml turns into ESC (measured). The pass side is the same value single-quoted, where YAML keeps the backslash as text: a rule that matched the characters anywhere would fail every shell colour in a workflow run block, which is literal there too.

regras.titulo: no known agent setting that runs a command or widens approval

porque.texto: A cloned repository can carry the settings an AI client obeys before anyone types a command: a helper that runs in a non-interactive session, an environment block that sends the client's API traffic and credential to another host, a task that starts when the folder opens, a rule that approves every shell command. Each shipped as an advisory: CVE-2025-53773 (a workspace auto-approve key), CVE-2026-21852 (a project environment block redirecting the API endpoint), CVE-2025-61260 (a dotenv file moving an agent home into the repository), CVE-2026-41613 (a loader variable in an MCP server environment). In a diff they all look like configuration.

The files are PARSED, not grepped: a key with one letter written as a unicode escape, behind a comment and a trailing comma, is invisible to a text pattern and real to the editor. A duplicate key fails on its own, because clients disagree about which copy wins. Command text, URLs and header values are printed only as a sha256 prefix and a length.

Settings that wait for folder trust, or that a team uses on purpose, pass with a warning instead: hooks, plugin marketplaces, the preview launch file. An accepted setting is pinned in `.rebar-injection-allowlist` by file, pointer and the hash of its value.

provas.porque: The permission default of a tracked Claude settings file. The fail side sets the mode that stops asking before any tool runs: current clients ignore it from a project file and older ones honored it, and removing it costs nothing, so it fails. The pass side sets the planning mode, which asks more, not less. Every content is base64, so no tracked file of this repository holds a live settings key. Whoever drops the mode check turns the fail side green; whoever fails on any mode value turns the pass side red.

Codex permission profiles replace the sandbox mode, and the built-in no-sandbox profile set as the default of a project config removes the sandbox for everyone who trusts the project. The fail side sets it. The pass side selects the workspace profile. Whoever reads only the older sandbox key passes the fail side.

A project Codex config is TOML, so the rule parses TOML rather than grepping a line. The fail side sets the approval policy that never asks before a command runs, which applies to everyone who trusts the project. The pass side sets the policy that asks on request. Whoever matches only a quoted JSON key passes the fail side.

The containers.dev spec lets a repository keep several dev containers as .devcontainer/<folder>/devcontainer.json, one folder deep, and the Dev Containers extension writes customizations.vscode.settings into the container. Main read only .devcontainer/devcontainer.json, so the chat auto-approve key in a subfolder config was not applicable. Both sides track .devcontainer/python/devcontainer.json; the pass side turns auto-approve off and the fail side turns it on. Without the subfolder route the pass side is na instead of passou and the fail side is na instead of reprovou.

A tracked .env that moves an agent home to a relative folder makes the client load its configuration from the repository (CVE-2025-61260). The fail side does it. The pass side tracks an example env file with the same line, which is the documented fix and not read, plus a real .env with a harmless port, so the rule runs and finds nothing. Whoever reads every .env* name fails the pass side.

A .env stored in Git LFS has a pointer in the index and its real content only in a smudged checkout, which is what the client loads. A .env is not an agent file, so the reader names no reading problem for it, and the pointer text holds no variable: the rule passed with nothing to say. The fail side tracks .gitattributes routing .env through LFS and a pointer in place of .env. The pass side tracks the same .gitattributes and a plain .env with a harmless port. Read the pointer as an ordinary .env and the fail side goes green.

JSON.parse keeps the last of two equal keys, and other parsers keep the first, so a duplicated key is where two clients read two different settings. The fail side defines the same permission default twice, both times with the harmless default value, and still fails: the disagreement is the defect, whatever the values are today. The pass side defines it once. A duplicate is never exemptable.

Claude Code rules for deno fmt, a named deno task, pwsh -File with a fixed script, node --run with a script name and npm --version reach no arbitrary command: fmt runs only built-in formatters, words after a task name go to the task (deno cli_parser tests), everything after the script goes to the script (measured with Windows PowerShell 5.1), node --run runs a package.json script like npm run, and --version prints and exits whatever follows (measured on npm 11.6.2). Main judged all five broad while the npm run and python script equivalents passed. The pass side allows exactly those five. The fail side allows every deno task, where --eval runs any text. Reading these shapes as broad turns the pass side red; reading deno task as narrow without its name turns the fail side green.

The env block of a tracked Claude settings file is applied at startup of a non-interactive run. The fail side points the client API base address at another host, which sends the credential along (CVE-2026-21852). The pass side sets a telemetry exporter endpoint, which is a warning only: the verdict passes and the nota names it. Whoever reads env names by a loose suffix match fails the pass side; whoever stops reading the env block passes the fail side.

The allowed tools of a skill are applied whenever the skill runs, with no folder trust asked, in a non-interactive run too. The fail side grants the bare shell tool, which is every command. The pass side grants one exact npm script plus a read tool, which is a warning only. The frontmatter is read by a YAML parser, so a list and a spaced string are the same grant.

Claude settings are strict JSON: a trailing comma makes the client skip the file, while tolerant editor parsers still apply part of it, so the rule cannot vouch for what any client runs and fails the file. The fail side has one trailing comma; the pass side is the same object without it. An unparseable file is never exemptable.

A VS Code task set to start by itself when the folder opens runs a repository command with no one asking for it; forks that ship workspace trust off run it at once. The fail side declares that run option; the pass side declares the same task without it. The key sits under the run options object, not at the top of the task, which is the path the plan first got wrong.

regras.titulo: every MCP server launch in versioned config is the template or allowlisted

porque.texto: A versioned MCP configuration is a program the client starts on the developer's machine, and headless and cloud sessions load project servers without asking. An allowlist by server NAME was measured against real history and lost both ways: it fired on 149 of 150 routine version bumps, and a server renamed in the same commit as its new command walked past it.

So a launch is judged by a sha256 fingerprint of every field that decides what runs. The one launch accepted with no entry is the template this rebar ships, read from the running package and never from the target: rebar-site, assay and navesz-portfolio track it byte for byte. Any other launch needs its fingerprint in `.rebar-injection-allowlist`.

Some findings no entry can accept, because they change what runs without changing the text: an unparseable file or a duplicate key, a command read from the environment, a server marked trusted, the mcp-remote proxy below
0.1.16 (CVE-2025-6514, CVSS 9.6), and a package runner next to a tracked registry override.

explicacoes: a runner that downloads an npm or git package and starts it
a runner that downloads a Python package and starts it
a container engine that pulls an image and starts it
Deno, which can start a module fetched from the network
a POSIX shell handed an inline command string

provas.porque: A versioned .mcp.json is a program the client starts: Claude Code loads project servers without asking in headless, Agent SDK and cloud sessions.The pass side is new/gate/arquivos/mcp.json byte for byte, the launch rebar-site, assay and navesz-portfolio track today, and it needs no allowlist entry because the running rebar ships it. The fail side adds one server that connects to a remote URL. Whoever drops the implicit template acceptance turns the pass side red (and three live CIs with it); whoever judges only stdio commands, or only known-bad hosts, lets the fail side through.

An allowlist that accepts a server by NAME accepts whatever that name launches next: measured on real history, a name-based check fired on 149 of 150 routine bumps and missed a server renamed together with its new command. Both sides track the same .rebar-injection-allowlist line, which carries the sha256 fingerprint of one exact launch of a remote npm package. The pass side launches exactly that; the fail side keeps the server name and changes only the package version. Whoever matches entries by arquivo and servidor alone turns the fail side green; whoever breaks the canonical fingerprint turns the pass side red.

Codex reads MCP servers from [mcp_servers.<name>] tables in .codex/config.toml, a format no JSON reader sees. The fail side declares one server that downloads a Python package and starts it, with no acceptance; the pass side is the same file plus its exact fingerprint in .rebar-injection-allowlist. Whoever leaves TOML out turns the fail side into not-applicable; whoever fingerprints a TOML server differently from the same launch in JSON turns the pass side red.

VS Code starts the MCP servers a dev container declares under customizations.vscode.mcp, the place its docs name, and one repository can keep several containers one folder down. The fail side declares a server launched through a shell in such a subfolder config. The pass side accepts that exact launch by its fingerprint, and passes with a warning. Whoever reads only .vscode/mcp.json turns the fail side not applicable.

Gemini settings with trust set to true skip every tool confirmation for that server, which no review of the launch text can make safe. Both sides track a .rebar-injection-allowlist line carrying the exact fingerprint of their own server, so the entry matches on both. The fail side sets trust to true and must still fail; the pass side sets it to false and passes through its entry. Whoever lets an allowlist entry exempt trust turns the fail side green; whoever fails every Gemini server regardless of trust turns the pass side red.

A package runner next to a registry override cannot be accepted by fingerprint, because the override changes which package the same text starts. Only an override that changes where THIS launch resolves its package counts. Both sides track the same allowlisted npx launch of a scoped package. The pass side also tracks a root .npmrc that names the public default registry and routes an unrelated company scope elsewhere, and a nested package .npmrc with a private registry that a launch from the root never reads: measured before, each of those made the launch unexemptable. The fail side tracks a root .npmrc that routes the launched package scope to another registry. Whoever counts every registry line anywhere turns the pass side red; whoever ignores scoped overrides turns the fail side green. Content is base64 because rebar reads its own caso.json raw.

npm reads .npmrc with the ini parser: a quoted key is the key, and an inline comment after a value is not part of it (measured with npm 11.6.2 npm config get). Main read the file line by line with a regular expression, so a quoted registry key pointing npx at another host passed next to an allowlisted launch, while the public default registry followed by a comment made the launch unexemptable. Both sides track the same .mcp.json launch and its allowlist line. The pass side .npmrc names the default registry with an inline comment; the fail side sets the quoted registry key to another host. Without the ini reading the pass side goes red and the fail side goes green.

The mcp-remote proxy below 0.1.16 carries CVE-2025-6514 (CVSS 9.6), so no allowlist entry may accept it. A codeload or GitHub archive link, a repository URL and an npm alias name the same package without the bare name the rule looked for, and an entry with their fingerprint accepted 0.1.10. Both sides track one allowlisted npx launch whose package spec is a codeload tarball link of mcp-remote. The pass side links tag v0.1.16, a version the rule can read; the fail side links tag v0.1.10. Whoever reads only bare names turns the fail side green; whoever refuses every URL spec turns the pass side red. Content is base64 because rebar reads its own caso.json raw.

A server started through a shell with an inline command string runs anything the string says, and the string is where an attacker edits. The fail side launches a POSIX shell with an inline command and no acceptance, so it fails with the shell label. The pass side is the same launch with its exact fingerprint in .rebar-injection-allowlist: a shell launch is reviewed and accepted, it is not one of the findings no entry can exempt. Whoever skips commands that are not package runners turns the fail side green; whoever makes the shell label unexemptable turns the pass side red.

VS Code keeps its servers under "servers", not "mcpServers", and reads .vscode/mcp.json with comments and trailing commas. A reader that only knows mcpServers misses every VS Code server, and a strict JSON reader calls the file unparseable. The fail side is such a file with one unaccepted local server; the pass side is the same file plus its exact fingerprint in .rebar-injection-allowlist. Whoever reads only mcpServers turns the fail side into not-applicable; whoever parses it as strict JSON turns the pass side red.

A VS Code workspace file declares MCP servers under settings.mcp, which the VS Code resource scanner reads. The fail side points one there at a remote address. The pass side writes the same map at the top level of the file, which VS Code never reads, so no configuration is tracked. Whoever reads the top-level key fails the pass side; whoever reads no workspace file passes the fail side.

regras.titulo: no agent CLI started with its approval switch turned off

porque.texto: Two supply-chain incidents used exactly this shape. The Nx s1ngularity release (August 2025) shipped an install script that looked for agent CLIs on the machine and started each one with its permission prompts skipped, asking it to search the disk for wallets and keys. The Amazon Q Developer extension 1.84.0 (CVE-2025-8217) carried a line that started the vendor's chat CLI with every tool trusted and a prompt that wiped files and cloud resources. The switch was the whole difference between an agent that asks and an agent that acts.

The place decides the verdict, not the switch alone: 25 of 39 sampled GitHub Agentic Workflows lock files carry such switches inside a firewall container, on purpose. It fails where nothing asks a person first: package lifecycle scripts and the files they start, git hooks, editor tasks that run on folder open, agent hooks, agent instruction files, and workflows that are not generated lock files (a workflow that only runs on push or on a schedule included). Elsewhere it is a warning.
Most switches are one letter or a generic word, so they count only with their binary in the same command, or within 3 lines in code. The output names the CLI and the effect, never the switch.

provas.porque: The Nx s1ngularity release (August 2025) shipped a postinstall that started every agent CLI it found with the switch that skips permission prompts, and handed it a prompt that searched the disk for wallets and keys. npm runs a postinstall on every install with no dialog. The fail side is that shape: a package.json whose postinstall starts Claude Code with the strong skip switch. The pass side keeps the same postinstall slot busy with the two measured look-alikes that are not a bypass: a package runner told not to prompt, and Claude Code in print mode with no approval switch, plus grep and ls short switches in an ordinary script. Whoever makes a short switch accuse without its binary turns the pass side red; whoever stops reading lifecycle scripts, or demands the binary next to a strong flag, turns the fail side green. Content is base64 because rebar reads its own caso.json raw.

The Codex action takes its sandbox as an input, not as a switch on a run line, so a rule that needs the binary and the switch in one command never saw it. The fail side sets the no-sandbox value in a push workflow. The pass side keeps the workspace sandbox and carries a config override for the sandbox in codex-args, which the action overrides with its own choice, so it passes. Whoever ignores action inputs passes the fail side; whoever greps codex-args fails the pass side.

The Claude Code action writes its settings input into the user settings file, where the default permission mode applies. The fail side sets the mode that approves every tool call, in a block scalar of a push workflow. The pass side sets the mode that accepts file edits. Whoever ignores the settings input passes the fail side; whoever fails any default mode fails the pass side.

An ambiguous switch in code counts only with its binary within 3 lines, the distance the Nx map needed between its cmd and args keys; further than that, a generic switch and an unrelated name are two different things. Both sides run src/a.mjs from a postinstall, so any finding would fail. On the fail side the Codex binary and its ambiguous approval switch are exactly 3 lines apart; on the pass side they are 5 lines apart and nothing is found. Whoever widens the window without measuring turns the pass side red; whoever narrows it below the Nx shape turns the fail side green.

Codex overrides any key of its config for one run with -c key=value, and the sandbox key set to no sandbox is the same hole as the sandbox switch. The fail side starts Codex that way from a postinstall, the Nx shape. The pass side overrides the approval policy with its never value, which the Codex config reference recommends for non-interactive runs, so it is not counted. Whoever reads only switches passes the fail side; whoever counts every override fails the pass side.

GitHub Agentic Workflows compiles every workflow into a lock file that starts the agent with its approval switch off inside a firewall container: 10 of 10 sampled Codex locks and 15 of 15 Copilot locks carry it. Failing those would fail every gh-aw adopter, so a lock file is only a warning (passed with a note). A lock is recognised by what the compiler writes, not by its comment: a .lock.yml name, the generated header, and activation and agent jobs with the agent needing the activation, the shape of all 24 lock files of the corpora. The fail side pastes the header and a roles comment above a plain workflow, which the review showed lowered it to a warning. Whoever skips lock files silently, fails them, or trusts the comment turns one side the wrong colour.

A git hook runs with no dialog, and so does a package script it calls by name. Main found the name with a regular expression that took an option after run as the script name, so .husky/pre-commit with npm run --silent ai left the ai script, which starts an agent CLI with its approval switch off, a warning; npm run ai failed. Both sides track the same package.json, whose ai script is that invocation and whose lint script is not. The pass side hook runs npm run --silent lint, so ai stays a warning; the fail side hook runs npm run --silent ai. Reading the option as the name turns the fail side green; following every script of a package a hook touches turns the pass side red.

An agent reads its instruction file whole, fenced blocks included, and a fenced command in AGENTS.md is an instruction to run it. The fail side is AGENTS.md with a sh fence that starts the Gemini CLI with its approval switch off. The pass side puts the byte-identical text in docs/setup.md, a document no agent loads by name: a fenced command there is only a warning (passed with a note), and the same words in prose would be nothing. Whoever skips fences in agent files turns the fail side green; whoever fails fenced examples in ordinary docs turns the pass side red.

The plan listed the Codex full-auto switch as a bypass. It is not: it means on-request approvals inside the workspace-write sandbox, and codex exec dropped its handling on 2026-07-30 (openai/codex commit 1c5f336c4). A workflow that runs Codex that way passes. The fail side is the same step with the Codex alias that turns off both approvals and the sandbox, next to its binary. Whoever adds full-auto back to the table turns the pass side red; whoever stops reading workflows turns the fail side green.

StepSecurity's write-up of the Nx postinstall shows the real code: the binary and the approval switch sit in separate string literals of a map, so a matcher that only looks inside one shell command misses it. Both sides track the same scripts/t.js, which names the Gemini binary on one line and passes its ambiguous approval switch two lines below. On the fail side the postinstall runs it with node, so the file is read with the 3-line code window and fails. On the pass side only the lint script runs it, and the same file is a warning (passed with a note). Whoever stops following node <file> from a lifecycle script, or drops the window, turns the fail side green; whoever fails every code file with a flag turns the pass side red.

Node loads the module named by its preload option (-r, --require, --import, --loader) before the entry, so the file behind it runs exactly as an entry does. The rule skipped that value as an option value, and a postinstall that preloads a tracked file whose code starts the Claude Code CLI with its permission prompts skipped passed with a note. Both sides track the same scripts/t.js. On the fail side the postinstall preloads it and names no entry; on the pass side only the lint script preloads it, which a person starts on purpose, and the file is a warning. Whoever skips the preload value turns the fail side green; whoever fails every code file with the switch turns the pass side red. Content is base64 because rebar reads its own caso.json raw.

A shell hands a quoted prompt to the program as one argument. Read as plain text, a dashed word of the prompt (a list switch of ls, a recursive-force switch of rm, a type switch of find) matched the one-letter approval group of the CLI in front of it, and honest workflows failed; and a separator inside a quoted URL cut the CLI from the approval switch that follows the URL, so that workflow passed with no note. The pass side is a workflow whose agent steps quote prompts holding those dashed words, and a URL with an ampersand and no switch. The fail side is a workflow whose step quotes a URL with an ampersand and then passes the long approval switch, unquoted, in the same command. Whoever reads quotes as plain text turns both sides wrong: the pass side red and the fail side green. Content is base64 because rebar reads its own caso.json raw.

The shell ends a word at a redirection or background operator and hands the word on unchanged, so a skip switch glued to `>` still reaches the CLI. Measured before the fix: a postinstall that started Claude Code with its strong skip switch written right before `>/dev/null` passed with no note, while the same line with a space before the operator failed. The fail side is that postinstall. The pass side glues the same operator to a print-mode call with no switch in the postinstall, and keeps the glued switch only in an ordinary lint script, which warns. Whoever drops the operators from the token edges turns the fail side green; whoever reads the operator itself as a switch turns the pass side red. Content is base64 because rebar reads its own caso.json raw.

The Gemini CLI parses its arguments with yargs, which expands a group of short options into each of them: the sandbox and approval short switches written as one single-dash word turn approval off exactly as the two words do (measured with yargs-parser 21.1.1 and the option shape of the CLI). Before the fix the rule matched only the exact one-letter word, so the grouped spelling in a postinstall passed with no note. The fail side is that postinstall. The pass side runs the CLI in the same postinstall with a group of debug and prompt switches, which holds no approval letter, and keeps the approval group in an ordinary lint script, which warns. Whoever matches only the exact word turns the fail side green; whoever fails any single-dash group next to the binary turns the pass side red. Content is base64 because rebar reads its own caso.json raw.

regras.titulo: no AI agent step in a workflow that outside text reaches with power to act

porque.texto: An agent step in a GitHub workflow reads the issue, comment or pull request that started it, and any account can write that text. PromptPwnd (Aikido, 2025-12-04) steered the Gemini CLI in Google's own triage workflows with a new issue. Clinejection (Adnan Khan, 2026-02-09) led Claude Code, running with a shell grant on an issue trigger, from an issue title to a poisoned Actions cache that reached release tokens. Comment and Control (2026-04-15) did it from a comment. The GitHub Security Lab keeps the list of event fields whose text is untrusted.

A step is exposed when a trigger any account can fire reaches it and its actor check is absent or opened by an input. Interpolated event text is reported, not required: 11 of 13 vendor examples on those triggers interpolate none, because the agent loads the text by itself. Conditions are evaluated per trigger, and a condition this rule cannot decide keeps the step reachable.

The verdict follows what the agent can reach. One that can run commands fails at any permission level; one the vendor keeps from commands and its own environment is a warning; anything else fails with a write scope beyond issues, pull requests and discussions, with no permissions block, or with a secret other than its model credential. Its text output spliced into a later script fails too. Measured over 1,660 workflows of agent adopters, each with its own repository as the origin: 150 steps fail, 126 of them with execution or code injection (170 with no origin, where copies of a workflow gated on another repository's name stay reachable). Over the 29 workflows of 24 local repositories, the rebar worktree and the gate template: none. Of 3,292 real workflows 6 use YAML anchors, and 2 of those hide an agent step behind an alias, so aliases are read.

provas.porque: An AI agent step on a trigger any account can fire is only as safe as what it can act with. Both sides run the Claude Code action on a new issue with contents write. The pass side keeps the action default, which runs only for accounts with write access, so outside text never steers it. The fail side opens that check to every account and grants the agent a whole shell: anyone who opens an issue can make it run commands with the job token (the Clinejection shape). Whoever ignores the actor check fails the pass side; whoever needs event text interpolated passes the fail side, since the action reads the issue by itself.

A team that accepts an exposed agent pins that exact workflow blob in .rebar-injection-allowlist. Both sides track the failing workflow of the base case; the pass side adds its file and blob id, and passes with a warning that no CODEOWNERS entry guards the list. Whoever ignores the allowlist fails the pass side; whoever matches by path alone would accept the next edit too.

GitHub reads YAML anchors and aliases in workflows, and two of six real workflows that use them hide an agent step behind one. The fail side names the agent action through an alias on a new issue, with a whole shell. The pass side is the same file started only by hand. Whoever refuses the alias as unreadable or skips it passes or breaks the fail side; whoever fails any agent regardless of trigger fails the pass side.

The Codex action checks write access unless an input opens it, and keeps the agent in a sandbox with sudo dropped. Both sides open it to every account on pull_request_target with contents write. The fail side also takes the sandbox away, so a fork author steers an agent that runs anything. The pass side keeps the read-only sandbox under the default strategy, and passes with a warning. Whoever fails every exposed Codex step fails the pass side; whoever ignores the sandbox input passes the fail side.

A gh-aw lock file carries its own role check, so the rule never judges it step by step, and it has to know a lock by what the compiler writes. The pass side, not applicable because no step of a lock is judged, is a lock on new issues whose agent job needs the activation job, which needs a role-check job whose step env admits admins, maintainers and writers. The fail side pastes the gh-aw header and a roles comment above a plain workflow that runs a base action with every permission prompt skipped under write-all on new issues; the review showed those two comment lines silenced the rule. Whoever judges locks step by step fails the pass side; whoever trusts the header passes the fail side.

A here-document body is data for the program it feeds, and commands only when a shell reads it. Both sides run on new issues with a bot token and no permissions block. The pass side, not applicable because it starts no agent, writes a welcome note through cat, and the note mentions an agent command in backticks; the review measured that shape taken for an agent launch in a real workflow. The fail side feeds the same kind of body to bash, whose line starts the agent CLI. Whoever reads every body line as a command fails the pass side; whoever skips every body passes the fail side.

A job condition that admits only owners and members closes an agent to outside comments, and the rule has to read it per trigger. The pass side runs a base action with a whole shell on issue comments behind that condition. The fail side adds the issues trigger and ORs the same condition with the event being issues, which lets any account in by opening an issue. Whoever ignores conditions fails the pass side; whoever reads a condition as passed when any operand passes misses the fail side.

The inputs context exists only for workflow_dispatch and workflow_call; on an issue comment it is null, and null compares equal to an empty string. The pass side lets the agent run when a dispatch input is not empty or the commenter is an owner, which on a comment leaves only owners. The fail side tests the input for being empty, which on every comment is true and admits any account. Whoever leaves the inputs atom undecided fails the pass side; whoever decides it the wrong way passes the fail side.

The not-applicable branches: a repository with no workflow, and a workflow with no known agent step, have nothing this rule judges, and silence by absence must not become passed (invariant I4). The pass side tracks a checkout-only workflow; the fail side tracks no workflow at all. Both must say na.

The old GitHub starter summary workflow put the model response inside a quoted shell string of the next step, so a response that closes the quote runs as shell with the job token: the agent writes the injection. The fail side is that shape. The pass side hands the same response over through env, as the current starter does, and passes with a warning. Whoever reads only the agent step passes the fail side.

PromptPwnd (Aikido, December 2025) steered the Gemini CLI inside Google triage workflows with the title and body of a new issue: the action approves every tool call, and the tool list held a shell command scoped to editing issues. The fail side is that shape. The pass side gives the agent an empty core tool list and no MCP server, and passes its summary to the next step through env, so the step passes with a warning. Whoever treats a scoped shell tool as harmless passes the fail side; whoever fails every exposed agent fails the pass side.

A local reusable workflow runs with the trigger of the workflow that calls it. The fail side calls one from issue comments with every secret inherited, and the callee starts the Gemini CLI action with no tool list, fed the comment through an input. The pass side is the same pair started only by hand. Whoever judges the callee by its own workflow_call trigger passes the fail side.

A job that needs a gate job runs as success() && (its if) unless its if calls a status function, in any letter case, and success() is false once the gate was skipped (actions/runner PipelineTemplateConverter). The pass side keeps an owner-only gate in front of a base action with a whole shell and calls success() itself, which still needs the gate. The fail side calls Always() in capitals, which runs the agent after the gate skipped for an outside comment; the review showed it read as closed. Whoever ignores the gate job fails the pass side; whoever matches status functions by lowercase text passes the fail side.

A YAML feature this rule does not read cannot hide an agent. Both sides carry an explicit tag the reader refuses. The fail side names an agent action in that file, so it fails closed. The pass side names none and passes with a warning that says which file was not read. Whoever skips unreadable files passes the fail side; whoever fails every unreadable file fails the pass side.

The runner splits a uses value at slashes and backslashes and drops the empty parts, so a doubled slash still names the same folder of the action repository. The pass side runs the Claude Code action itself, which runs only for accounts with write access, with a whole shell on new issues. The fail side names its base action with a doubled slash before the folder: the runner starts the base action, which checks no actor, and the review showed the rule read it as the gated action. Whoever ignores the actor check fails the pass side; whoever matches the raw uses text passes the fail side.

A workflow_run job runs with the base secrets after another workflow, whoever started that one. The fail side runs an agent with a whole shell after CI, and CI runs on pull requests, which any fork can open. The pass side is the same pair with CI running only on push. Whoever treats workflow_run as safe passes the fail side; whoever never resolves the upstream fails the pass side.

regras.titulo: no escaped terminal control in an MCP server file

porque.texto: Trail of Bits showed terminal control sequences inside MCP tool descriptions, hidden from the person using a coding agent and read in full by the model, written in the server source as ESCAPES rather than raw bytes, which control-bytes cannot see.

Where a description string begins and ends cannot be found without running the server: descriptions are built by concatenation, joins, interpolation and schema helpers. So this works per file. A candidate is a code file that uses an MCP server SDK, or a tracked file a versioned MCP config launches; the finding is an escaped ESC or CSI in its code, comments stripped.
A heuristic at N1 because an honest server may colour a console line: measured, 2 of 48 unique server files in node_modules did. It informs, and fails only under `--heuristics`.
